While the recent Fitbit Edge and screen-less Fitbit Air are the hottest fitness trackers of 2026, Samsung appears set to launch a direct competitor to the former in the near-ish future.

The Samsung Galaxy Fit 4 would replace 2024’s Samsung Galaxy Fit 3, a small tracker with a large display and support for some of Samsung’s best holistic tools, borrowed from the higher-end Galaxy Watch line.

What might the Galaxy Fit 4 bring to the table, and will it be enough to beat the Fitbit Edge, arguably the best fitness tracker for most people on the market today? Here’s everything we know (and think we know) about the Galaxy Fit 4 based on recent rumors and leaks.

The Samsung Galaxy Fit 3 debuted globally in 2024 but wasn’t available in the U.S. until winter 2025. A launch price of $59 made the Galaxy Fit 3 one of the best bang-for-your-buck fitness trackers on the market at the time, undercutting even the popular Fitbit Inspire 3.

I’ve yet to see any pricing rumors for the Galaxy Fit 4, but based on its predecessor's cost and Samsung’s history of beating the competition, price-wise, I’d be willing to bet that the Galaxy Fit 4 is a little more than the Galaxy Fit 3 (to account for inflation, at least) but still less than the $99 Fitbit Air.

Based on leaked blueprints of the device from earlier this year, first shared by Android Authority, the Galaxy Fit 4 is tipped to feature a rectangular case with a decently sized AMOLED touchscreen and a single physical button on the side, just like its predecessor and the Fitbit Edge.

In terms of display specs, the older model features a rectangular 1.6-inch AMOLED panel with 256 x 402 pixels of resolution and a max brightness of around 600 nits. What might the Galaxy Fit 4 feature?

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

My guess is that the screen size will stay the same. However, according to a recently published report from SammyGuru — which allegedly previewed an unreleased version of the companion app — the new model will have a slightly higher-res 258 × 428-pixel display than its predecessor.

In terms of brightness, given advancements in display technology over the past few years, there’s a good chance the Galaxy Fit 4 will also offer a higher maximum brightness than its predecessor for better readability in bright daylight.

What about the overall aesthetic of the wearable? A mostly aluminum case is likely, and you can also probably expect at least three color options, including black and white, with either blue or green replacing the Galaxy Fit 3's pink model.

The Samsung Galaxy Fit 4 is slated to have the brand’s GH3036 health sensor array for continuous heart rate monitoring and other holistic tracking capabilities. This information comes from Samsung’s own documents, first reported on by Android Authority.

New stress tracking and management tools could be in the cards, based on more recent insider reports; automatic workout detection is also rumored.

But beyond basic health, sleep, and fitness tracking, there’s still a lot we don’t know about the Galaxy Fit 4, feature-wise. For example, will it gain GPS for location tracking without a paired phone or NFC for contactless payments? Its predecessor lacks both, and either would be a welcome upgrade.

Like the Galaxy Fit 3, I fully expect the new model to offer safety tools like fall detection and emergency SOS, along with important health monitoring features like instant blood oxygen saturation (SpO2) readings, daily sleep scores, high/low pulse notifications, and snore detection.

Another upgrade I’d like to see is the addition of sleep apnea detection, something you’ll find on the best Samsung watches but not the Galaxy Fit 3.

Finally, the Galaxy Fit 3 is rated at an impressive 13 days of battery per charge. With the Galaxy Fit 4, battery life will likely be comparable, that is, unless Samsung outfits the wearable with a power-hungry GPS antenna.

Even if the Samsung Galaxy Fit 4 gains GPS and NFC and sells for a lower price than the competition, namely Fitbit, one major factor could ultimately limit its popularity: lack of iOS support.

While Google’s top-of-the-line wearables like the Pixel Watch 5 are Android-only, the brand’s line of Fitbit fitness trackers all play nicely with both Android and iOS devices.

This is to say, if Samsung is serious about making a dent in Google’s dominance in the wallet-friendly fitness tracker market, making the Galaxy Fit 4 multi-platform would be a wise first step.

#3297. Reddit calls Australia’s under-16 social media ban ‘inept’ in court

The first legal challenge to the world-first ban says it tramples political speech without making teens safer.

Reddit’s venue in Cannes during Cannes Lions, 22 June 2026

Reddit has asked Australia’s High Court to strike down the country’s world-first ban on under-16s holding social media accounts, arguing that the law is unconstitutional. The first legal challenge to the legislation opened in Canberra this week, Reuters reported.

Reddit and a libertarian advocacy group say the ban violates an implied constitutional freedom of political communication.

Their lawyer, Perry Herzfeld, described the legislation as “ill thought out”, “inept” and a “profound restriction on political debate”.

The ban came into force in late 2025, requiring major platforms to prevent under-16s from holding accounts. Since then, the government has doubled the maximum penalty for breaches to A$99m ($69.5m).

It has also expanded the eSafety Commissioner’s powers to demand information and is preparing legal action to enforce the restrictions against major platforms.

Reddit says it supports efforts to protect children online but argues the legislation is ineffective. Herzfeld said the law does not specify clear steps platforms must take to keep minors off their services.

Also, it leaves out other online spaces where bullying takes place, including gaming platforms. Research by the eSafety Commissioner’s office has found that most under-16s continue to use social media.

The company also argues that it should not fall within the law’s scope. Reddit is organised around topic-based forums rather than networks of personal connections, and much of its content is accessible without an account.

The Australian government is defending the legislation, with communications minister Anika Wells named as a defendant.

Government lawyer Joanna Davidson told the seven High Court judges that children are more susceptible than adults to addictive platform features because their brains are still developing. She is due to continue her arguments on Wednesday.

Wells has said she will defend the ban while respecting the court’s decision. The High Court’s ruling will be final and cannot be appealed.

The case is attracting attention well beyond Australia. Governments across Europe and Asia are considering their own age restrictions, while social media companies face growing legal scrutiny over the effects of their platforms on teenagers. In the US, that includes lawsuits over social media addiction.

#3296. This Hidden Device Could Free Up Gigawatts of Grid Power

The November issue of IEEE Spectrum is here!

Variable frequency drives can slash motors’ power use

Zurich-based ABB is one of several manufacturers of variable frequency drives (VFDs), such as this ACH580. VFDs could help make the millions of electric motors running in industrial facilities more energy efficient.

This article was originally published by Canary Media.

America’s energy supply crunch is driving a surge of federal and private investment in new electricity generation—from polluting gas turbines to cleaner developments like solar farms and geothermal plants. But gigawatts of power are already available for the taking across the U.S. economy in the form of wasted energy from an unexpected source: motors.

Some 50 million electric motors drive the fans, pumps, and compressors found in virtually every factory and building. Together, they gobble enough electricity to equal nearly a third of total U.S. power demand. Often, the motors use far more energy than they actually need to keep America’s machines humming.

Companies can install devices known as variable frequency drives, or VFDs, to make motors run super efficiently. Yet adoption remains relatively low, in part because of the perceived hassle of retrofitting equipment and because they’re typically not required. On average, only 16 percent of motor systems at industrial facilities and 4 percent of commercial-sector motors use VFDs, according to a 2021 market report by Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory.

However, there are now more reasons than ever to equip the nation’s motors with power-saving devices, energy experts and device manufacturers say. They’re urging federal agencies, utilities, and deep-pocketed tech giants to spur a wider rollout of VFDs through financial incentives and efficiency standards.

For one, slashing motors’ power use would free up grid capacity for large electricity users like data centers and electric vehicles, they argue. It would help curb costs for factories that are switching from fossil-fueled heating systems to electrified, motor-based solutions like heat pumps—all at a time when industrial power prices are climbing fast. Plus, VFD technology has become far more sophisticated and less expensive to install than earlier iterations.

“This is low-hanging fruit that gives a lot [of energy] back and is reasonably simple,” Nik Sawe, a senior policy analyst at the nonpartisan think tank Energy Innovation, says of the technology.

Energy-wise, the main problem with electric motors is that they’re always running at full capacity. Consider an office building, which empties out in the evening. The heating, ventilation, and air-conditioning system can wind down in those hours, with dampers and valves restricting the flow of cold or hot air. But the motors and fans that drive the whole setup are still working in the background, wasting energy.

VFD technology, such as the Danfoss iC7 series, has gained some momentum in recent years among factories and buildings trying to combat rising electricity costs. Danfoss Drives

VFDs are electronic controllers with temperature sensors that continually adjust the speed of motors, automatically ramping up or down to match demand. The technology, which is also called adjustable speed drives, has the potential to curb a motor’s energy use by around 40 to 60 percent, says Neal Elliott, director emeritus of the American Council for an Energy-Efficient Economy.

All those energy reductions add up. Toyota, for example, installed VFDs on over 200 motors inside the HVAC system at its auto manufacturing plant in Georgetown, Kentucky, as part of a US $1.25 million pilot project in 2015. The automaker saved more than $700,000 in annual electricity costs thanks to the VFDs, and it continues to use the technology at other manufacturing facilities across the U.S., the company said by email.

“We’ve known for many, many years that there’s a huge opportunity for energy savings by varying the speed of the motor,” says Elliott, who noted that he literally wrote the book on energy-efficient motor systems in 2002.

Certain aspects of the technology have historically held the drives back since they debuted in the late 1960s. Measuring the flow of water, air, refrigerant—whatever is moving through the system that the motors are driving—was for decades an expensive engineering process. Accurately controlling motors to deliver the right amount of juice, at just the right time, faced similar issues.

But recent advances in sensors and machine-learning algorithms have significantly slashed the cost and complexity of using drives, Elliott says. Modern VFDs have also benefited from the increased production of advanced power chips that are used in high-voltage applications such as electric vehicles and solar power inverters.

Another long-standing challenge has been that commercial and industrial building developers often prioritize reducing upfront costs over netting long-term energy savings, and so they don’t always build to the highest efficiency levels, says Zack Valdez, senior director of regulatory and industry affairs at the National Electrical Manufacturers Association, whose members include drive and motor makers.

“If the facility that you’re putting it into doesn’t require it, then oftentimes people will overlook [VFDs], because they’re just trying to build to a minimum set of energy requirements,” he says. And if companies don’t install drives from the start, they’re likely less inclined to take time to retrofit an operating system.

The trade association recently launched a pilot program with manufacturers, utilities, and energy-efficiency groups to collect real-world data about how VFDs reduce motors’ electricity use and lower utility bills. The goal is to demonstrate how the technology can benefit not only individual facilities but also the wider grid—giving utilities a concrete reason to provide rebates for industrial customers.

Proponents say they hope the results will help the U.S. Department of Energy shape future efficiency measures and incentives that encourage adoption of the drives, including in federally owned buildings. Despite the Trump administration’s open hostility toward home appliance and equipment mandates, agency staff have apparently been receptive to discussing solutions that could meet the soaring power needs of data centers.

“If you added a drive to all the motors that are out there, you could provide [power for] up to five years of data center growth without having to build any new generation,” says Kirk Anderson, director of government relations and public affairs for ABB. The global manufacturing giant makes VFDs domestically near Milwaukee.

Anderson floated the idea of having tech companies help pay for factory owners to install VFDs to free up room on the grid. After all, hyperscalers are already spending many billions of dollars to revive shuttered nuclear plants, support next-generation geothermal projects, deploy fleets of grid-scale batteries, and supercharge the build-out of gas turbines and power plants.

“Instead of ‘bring your own power,’ it should be ‘offset your own power,’” he says, referring to a growing effort by states to get data centers to secure their own power resources and prevent rising costs for regular customers.

Michael Reckamp, the director of enterprise strategy for Danfoss Drives, North America, another VFD manufacturer, said that despite the traditionally low adoption rates, the technology has gained some momentum in recent years among factories and buildings as rising electricity costs and other grid-wide challenges make it harder to justify wasting energy.

Still, “it hasn’t permeated enough to get everyone utilizing it,” he says. “In the current situation, where we’re having so many issues with grids, brownouts, and now data centers wanting to take the load, I think there should be a renewed focus on putting drives out there to really reduce the stress on the grid and improve energy savings.”

Maria Gallucci is a clean-energy reporter with Canary Media.

#3295. This 140W power station might be the ultimate charger for Apple users [Video]

I have tested and used countless charging stations over the years, and while many of them get the job done, I feel like there is always some sort of compromise. Whether it’s not enough power, lack of a certain port that I need, or slow wireless charging, I have yet to find one that truly checks every box for me. But over the last month, I have been using CUKTECH’s new 140W Powerstation, and it has nailed everything. It is a six-in-one desktop charger with a built-in retractable cable, magnetic wireless charging, and a dedicated diagnostic display, all in an aesthetic, compact package. Here is everything you need to know and why I think it’s worth considering.

Be sure to check out our hands-on video to see this CUKTECH 15 PowerStation in action!

At its core, the CUKTECH 15 PowerStation is a 140W GaN charger. It can charge one device at the full 140W, meaning it can charge your 16-in MacBook Pro PROLED XDR at max speed, or it can divvy up that power to charge up to six devices at once. It also offers a great combination of ports, a built-in cable, and multiple wireless charging options. You get:

Of course, the biggest selling point is the versatility of it all. You can charge your MacBook Pro with the main USB-C port, charge your iPad with the built-in cable, place your iPhone on the MagSafe charger, and place your AirPods on the wireless charging pad. After all of that, there are still more ports for other accessories that I use daily.

Do keep in mind that the 140W output is the total output, so if more devices are added, that output is shared across all the connected devices.

I am someone who is constantly switching between so many Apple devices. I switch between my iPad Pro and MacBook Pro all the time, and now that it is techtember, I am testing multiple iPhones at the same time, so I need to make sure all of my devices are charged up for when I need them. Not only that, but I also need a USB-A port for my camera battery charging station. So having a centralized hub to charge all of my devices is a MUST in my desk setup. So what immediately stands out to me about the CUKTECH 15 is how much functionality they were able to pack into this relatively compact charging station.

I am a huge fan of built-in retractable cables; they eliminate the need to remember to carry a USB-C cable, so you know you can charge at least one device. Then you add in the wireless magnetic charging stand that supports the new iPhone Duo and StandBy Mode, all while keeping the iPhone upright and visible. Also, when you set up that magnetic charging pad in the upright position, it reveals an AirPods Pro charger. The design is so well thought out.

The cherry on top of it all is the display. I love being able to see how fast something is charging. It allows me to see whether products meet their charging speed standards and how different devices are affected by their charge levels. CUKTECH was also smart to still include one USB-A port. Lots of companies have decided to omit that port because it is an old standard, but there are still plenty of older and wacky tech that uses USB-A, so the inclusion is appreciated. The only thing missing is a dedicated Apple Watch charger, but I just plug in my own when I need it.

The CUKTECH 15 140W Charging Station is available today on Amazon for $149. It has been out in Europe for a little while, but now it has finally made it to the US!

There are plenty of charging stations on the market, but CUKTECH’s 140W power station is the first to check off all the boxes for me. It’s compact, looks great, has all the ports and charging methods I need, and features a beautiful TFT display that lets me know things are charging as they should. If you use multiple devices throughout the day and need them charged at all times, this is worth considering.

What do you think? Is this something you would use? How many devices do you normally have on you? Let’s discuss below!

Apple should have been a lot more transparent about its plans

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

It's no secret that the iPhone Duo has been pretty hard to get hold of, despite the fact prices start at $2,000. The consensus has been that limited supply is the main factor, but Mark Gurman at Bloomberg has revealed a few more factors that could explain why you're having to wait so long for your own iPhone Duo.

One of the biggest factors is that, according to Gurman, Apple actually rushed the iPhone Duo to market. He claims Apple originally intended to wait until November to launch, and even then the foldable would initially only be released in the U.S. and China. Other regions would have to wait until later this year, or more likely into 2027.

In other words, Apple wasn't really prepared to meet the demand, which explains why the company admitted it was "nothing short of extraordinary" to see so many people try to get hold of one.

On top of that, Apple apparently decided that it was going to prioritize brick-and-mortar Apple Stores over the online purchasing experience. This means roughly 80% of Apple's supply of iPhone Duos were set aside for walk-in purchases over that first weekend of sales. This explains why launch-day deliveries and pickups all sold out within minutes of iPhone Duo pre-orders going live.

Apparently stores only had 50 to 250 units each, depending on their size and location. Gurman also notes high storage options and blue units were in particularly short supply — and you'd likely need to camp out to get your hands on one.

Plus, as is the case with any high-profile product launch, scalpers have been using bots to monitor the Apple website and buy up as much stock as they can. That includes reserving any units that do become available for in-store pickup.

Considering scalpers have become a plague over the past several years, Apple should have seen that coming. It's possible that the emphasis on in-store sales was an attempt to try and curb the use of bots and prevent the minority of would-be scalpers from stockpiling Duo units.

Considering scalpers have become a plague over the past several years, Apple should have seen that coming.

But that obviously doesn't work if a) Apple doesn't tell anyone what's going on and b) scalpers are still able to reserve devices for in-store pickup en masse. The lack of transparency is definitely exacerbating the problems of getting hold of an iPhone Duo.

If you're looking to get an iPhone Duo, your only real option is to be patient and wait for Apple, carriers and major retailers to get one to you. It's possible that you may be able to snatch one up for in-store pickup if you're vigilant (and fast), but when you're competing with bots that task becomes significantly harder.

Obviously the last thing you want to do is buy a scalper unit for an inflated price. Not only are you wasting your money, you're encouraging this kind of behavior — and the more scalpers are emboldened, the more they'll do. Stuff costs enough right now without scalpers inserting themselves as middle men.

#3293. Here’s how I’m solving the iPhone Duo kickstand problem, without any bulk

If you’re like me and bought an iPhone Duo, you’re likely a bit disappointed by the options on the market to prop it up on a table. Apple’s official $129 folio with kickstand is expensive, flimsy, and gets in the way of the outer display. MagSafe wallets that turn into kickstands are too tall for the back of the phone, and there aren’t many good third party cases yet.

That said, the perfect option for an iPhone Duo kickstand might’ve actually been hiding in plain sight all along.

The reason why I say it’s been hiding in plain sight is because this accessory isn’t actually designed for iPhone Duo, it works on all iPhones. It’s the PopSocket Low-Pro, a low profile MagSafe PopSocket with a ring that flips out and serves as a kickstand. It also works as a normal PopSocket if you’re interested in that.

This PopSocket has a few strengths on iPhone Duo:

On the last point, you might’ve heard from some iPhone Duo reviewers that the phone can’t really work on a MagSafe stand while unfolded, because the weight of the left half of the phone drags it down. I’m happy to report that this PopSocket actually largely fixes that. It’ll still slip slightly over a longer period of time, but it’s good enough to make the experience usable.

I tested this across multiple MagSafe stands of mine and the slippage issue is improved across the board when using the PopSocket Low-Pro.

My favorite advantage to the PopSocket Low-Pro is the fact that it improves the iPhone Duo experience greatly while still allowing you to rock the phone without a case. Given the fact that the iPhone Duo is already 11.3mm thick when it’s folded, I wasn’t jazzed about the idea of adding even more bulk to the phone.

The wireless charging speed and efficiency is expected to go down with more layers in between the magsafe magnets on the phone and the grip. With that said, sadly, this does worse than the Oh Snap grip/stand when it comes to wireless charging. The pop socket completely stops wirelessly charging if you have a case on, even Magsafe ones.

The Low-Pro is truly low profile, and can’t really be felt when you’re holding the phone. It protrudes a fair bit less than the camera bump does.

If you’re interested in purchasing a PopSocket Low-Pro, you can grab one on Amazon for $36-40 depending on the color option you’d like. Navy, Gun Metal, Black, Electric Fuschia, Teal, Carbon Lattice, Mint, and Tortoise are available for $40, while the Lilac and Orange colors are available for $36, a 10% discount.

#3292. Walmart Will Have Three Major Shopping Events This Holiday Season

If you're thinking of picking up any big-ticket items soon—whether for yourself or as a gift for someone on your list— I would advise you to wait until you see what retailers have in store for the holiday sales season, which will kick off in earnest in mid-November. Walmart is the first major retailer to announce its Black Friday and Cyber Monday plan for 2026, and they actually involve three major shopping events between now and the December holidays. H

As it did in 2025, Walmart will hold three sales between Nov. 12 and Dec. 2, as outlined in a recent press release. The sales will be both online and in-store, and will target a mix of Walmart+ members and general shoppers.

The events will take place on three different dates:

Walmart's Black Friday Deals Event 1: Nov. 12–15

Available online and in stores starting at 6 a.m. local time

Walmart+ members get six hours of early access beginning online at 12:01 a.m. ET on November 12

Walmart's Black Friday Deals Event 2: Nov. 23–29

Online only: Nov. 23 starting at 12:01 a.m. ET

Online and in stores: Nov. 27 starting at 6 a.m. local time

Walmart+ members get six hours of early access online beginning Nov. 23 at 12:01 a.m. ET

Walmart's Cyber Monday Deals Event: Nov. 30-Dec. 2

Walmart says that you can expect discounts on electronics, toys, fashion, beauty, home goods, gifts, and everyday essentials. Although the company doesn't provide much in the way of specifics in its press release, last year's sales included discounts on TCL TVs, Dyson vacuums, Dreo appliances, and toys from LEGO.

The holiday season will see major sales from the same list of retailers that compete for your dollars throughout the year—namely, Best Buy, Target, and Amazon. Each will have its own version of Black Friday and Cyber Monday sales. So far, only Walmart has revealed its plans.

In short, yes. Though they aren't quite as impactful as they once were, Black Friday and Cyber Monday sales offer discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. Whether it's a major purchase you've been saving up for or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts, especially on items like appliances and electronics. Last year's sales included categories such as tech, home improvement, and fitness.

Black Friday used to be when major retailers offered their best deals on expensive tech and appliances, while Cyber Monday was for cheaper tech and gave smaller businesses a chance to compete online. Now, however, the distinction is almost meaningless: Every major retailer offers sales on both days, which means the smart move is to know what you want, use price trackers to monitor the deals, and refer to our Black Friday coverage, where we do all the searching, curating, and price tracking for you.

#3291. CrowdStrike agrees to buy AI security startups Fiddler and Dreadnode

CrowdStrike’s deals will bring agent observability and automated AI security testing to its Falcon platform. It also launched a kill switch for rogue AI agents, available today.

George Kurtz, chief executive and founder of CrowdStrike.

CrowdStrike has agreed to buy two AI security companies, Fiddler AI and Dreadnode. It announced both on Tuesday at its Fal.Con Europe conference in Barcelona. Fiddler tracks what AI agents do and why. Dreadnode tests AI models, applications and agents for weaknesses before they go live.

CrowdStrike did not disclose the prices. It plans to pay mostly in cash, plus some stock with vesting conditions, according to the Fiddler and Dreadnode announcements. Both deals are expected to close in CrowdStrike’s fourth quarter of fiscal 2027, subject to customary closing conditions.

“When a regulator or your board asks what an agent did, saying ‘the model did it’ is not an answer,” said George Kurtz, CrowdStrike’s chief executive and founder. “Fiddler is the flight recorder for every agent: the observability to explain exactly what an agent did and why.”

CrowdStrike will sell Fiddler as Falcon Observe, part of its Falcon platform. It is due in the fourth quarter of fiscal 2027. CrowdStrike says it will let companies see what every agent did and why, and prove it stayed within its task. Fiddler’s purpose-built models can cut evaluation costs by up to 98%, according to the company.

“We started Fiddler to help enterprises answer a fundamental question: can I trust what my AI agents are doing?” said Krishna Gade, Fiddler’s chief executive and co-founder.

Dreadnode runs more than 100 known AI attack strategies, including jailbreaks and prompt injection. It targets models, agent reasoning loops, applications and MCP servers. It maps what it finds to frameworks such as the OWASP Top 10 for large language models, MITRE ATLAS and NIST’s AI Risk Management Framework. Its team will join CrowdStrike’s Cyber Superintelligence Lab. The testing product is due in the same quarter as Falcon Observe.

“AI fails in ways traditional testing was never designed to catch, and the people best equipped to find those failures think like attackers,” said Brad Palm, Dreadnode’s chief executive.

CrowdStrike also launched an AI Kill Switch in Falcon Guardian, its AI security product. If an agent goes rogue, a defender can stop it where it runs and block it from launching again. The switch also cuts the agent’s access to the company network. An authorised administrator triggers it, and every action is logged. The release says the sensor stops agents at the gateway first, and “soon” on the endpoint. Unlike the two acquisitions, the switch is available today.

“If one goes off course, the AI Kill Switch gives our security team the final say,” said Rick Orloff, chief information security officer at Everpure, a CrowdStrike customer.

On the same day, CrowdStrike said it is bringing Falcon Guardian inside Anthropic’s Claude Cowork. The Falcon sensor runs inside the virtual machine where Cowork’s agents execute code. The integration is in beta on macOS, with Windows support expected later in November, CrowdStrike wrote in a blog post.

On Monday, the first day of the conference, CrowdStrike announced security deals with Dell for its AI Factory with Nvidia, and with Dynatrace and CoreWeave. It also said 15 partners, including BT, Deutsche Telekom Security, Orange Cyberdefense and Telefónica, had joined Project QuiltWorks as it expands across Europe. The programme uses frontier AI models to help customers find and fix security risks.

In September, CrowdStrike put OpenAI in the product and launched multi-agent investigations. In October, it linked South Korean bank breaches to AI tools. The conference ends on Wednesday.

My backyard is looking spectacular with the autumnal tones of gold and russet leaves. And I don’t even mind as they drift onto my lawn, creating a beautiful carpet of color.

But while I’m happy for them to settle for a short while, I won’t leave them all through winter, because although I appreciate their current aesthetic, over time they’ll damage my lawn.

A light flurry of leaves is not so much of a problem, but once your lawn gets covered in a carpet of fallen leaves, it can harm its health if they are not removed.

A thick layer of leaves is an open invitation to fungal disease, as the decaying matter traps moisture, blocks airflow and starves the grass of sunlight. This dark and damp microclimate is the perfect environment for fungi to thrive.

The layer of fallen leaves acts like a blanket, holding in rain, dew and condensation. And once the leaves are left there for a prolonged period, snow mold, brown patch and leaf blight will develop.

If your lawn is lightly covered with leaves, you can leave them be. The wind may help disperse some, while the rest will decompose and add nutrients to the soil.

However, if your lawn is covered in a deep pile of leaves, there’s little chance of sunlight reaching the blades of grass, and the trapped moisture won't dry out. In this scenario, you need to grab a rake and remove the leaves to prevent disease from becoming rife. If you don’t fancy the workout that raking leaves provides or you want to save time, you could also opt for a leaf blower or lawn sweeper.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Besides being a magnet for fungal disease, if leaves are left on your lawn, they can also attract pests. The leaf canopy can provide cover, warmth, moisture, and, once the leaves break down, food.

This metal rake comes with an adjustable head that can expand from 7-23 inches to suit your task. This allows it to pick up large leaves, clippings and lawn debris with ease, and it's also small enough to fit under hedges.

Whether you choose to rake or mow over your leaves, always aim for dry conditions. But if the forecast doesn’t look promising, clear what you can anyway — leaving a layer of wet leaves will suffocate your lawn and invite disease.

If the leaf cover is light, rather than a thick carpet, mowing is the faster route. Just ensure the leaves aren’t soaked to avoid clogging your mower. Best of all, mowing your leaves turns them into a valuable organic mulch, putting the goodness back into your soil.

#3288. Three new iPad models are reportedly launching early next year, here’s what’s coming

After debuting the refreshed iPad mini with OLED this past week, Apple still has more in the pipeline for the rest of the iPad lineup in the first half of next year. That includes a new iPad Air, a new base iPad, and a new iPad Pro, according to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman.

To follow up the iPad mini refresh, Apple’s next iPad Air refresh will also gain OLED. It’ll likely stick with a 60Hz panel, and likely won’t make the switch from Touch ID to Face ID – but it’ll bring a nifty display upgrade to the iPad Air, a product that hasn’t had a major refresh since 2020.

In terms of chipset, while not confirmed, a jump from the M4 chip to the M5 chip is rather likely. It’ll also likely come with a higher price, likely around $799-899 for the base 11-inch model.

Next year, Apple will also finally update the base iPad for the first time since early 2025. It’ll upgrade it to the A19 chip and 8GB of RAM, finally enabling Apple Intelligence support on Apple’s cheapest iPad. It should also gain the N1 chip and the C1X modem for improved networking performance.

There shouldn’t be any screen or design upgrades with this iPad, at least as of now – though it could potentially see some refreshed color options.

With the iPad Pro, Apple will be adding a vapor chamber to the device, a feat it started last year with the iPhone 17 Pro. It probably won’t have any meaningful changes otherwise, except for a new chipset – likely M6 or potentially M7.

Hopefully, there’s some surprises in store with this device. The iPad Pro now starts at $1199 for an 11-inch model and $1499 for a 13-inch model. It’ll have been around 3 years since the last major revamp by the time Apple introduces the M6 model, and the company should probably do something to make it a more worthwhile refresh.

#3287. Six Fitness 'Rules' That Don't Actually Matter

I’ve learned a lot in my many years in the gym, and beginner-me would be shocked and appalled by the things present-me does during workouts. With the benefit of experience, I now do exercises I used to think one should “never” do, and I’ve broken pretty much every other rule besides.

I've already explained a bunch of things you can stop worrying about as a beginner, but I’d like to expand on that list with a few more rules that even intermediate-level exercisers can ditch without consequence.

If you can theoretically do 13 bicep curls with a certain weight, how many curls should you actually do? One common misconception is that if you don’t do all 13, you’re leaving gains on the table. The rule kind of makes sense if you have truly no clue where to start; if you go until you can’t do a single rep more, then at least you know you’re not slacking off.

But the downside is that going to failure for every set of every lift is just going to make you exhausted. On bicep curls, maybe not so much, but once you’re squatting pretty heavy weights, you’re going to feel spent if you do every single set to failure, and that fatigue will get in the way of getting a good workout in consistently. What’s better is to follow a program that advises you on when to hold back and when it’s a good time to really push your limits. You’ll find that most of the time, you stop a set at least 2-3 reps shy of failure, and sometimes even more.

Rest days are a convenient tool for making sure you’re not overworking yourself, but that’s all. Organizations like the American College of Sports Medicine recommend leaving 48 hours between intense strength-training sessions for a given muscle, but if you look at where they get that number, it’s meant to be a general recommendation for beginners and for people who are exercising just to stay healthy. Once you’re talking about athletes or enthusiasts, the ACSM acknowledges that training most days of the week is fine if your program manages fatigue effectively. That may mean alternating between heavier and lighter days, rather than taking complete rest days.

The “10% rule” is a not-terrible guideline for figuring out how quickly to ramp up your training. But like many of these other myths, it’s a suggestion, not a commandment to be strictly obeyed.

As running coach Jason Fitzgerald told Lifehacker, “While the adage is to only increase weekly mileage by 10%, this may be either too conservative or even too aggressive depending on where you start from.” When you’re coming back from a short layoff, you can probably increase mileage a lot faster. Same goes if you’re a beginner and your mileage is overall very low; if you took the rule literally, you wouldn’t be able to increase from zero to any other number.

Meanwhile, serious running programs—once again, a program is a wonderful thing—may give you a bigger increase for a few weeks in a row, then cut back and decrease your mileage temporarily before ramping up again. Or they may keep you at the same mileage for weeks at a time before venturing a larger increase. If you were to stick to the 10% rule, you would miss out on the advantages of programs that work this way.

There are pros and cons to lifting before cardio, and to doing cardio before lifting. It’s more of an “it depends” than a rule. So here are some of the ways to decide which makes sense.

Your lifts tend to suffer when you’re fatigued, and doing them fresh is important to you

Cardio is your top priority, and you want to have more energy for it

Your lifts are the kind of thing that can get done even when you’re fatigued

Or you only intend to do a small amount of cardio before lifting

So a cyclist may prefer to do a strength workout after hopping off the bike, but a powerlifter would probably rather get their conditioning in after finishing squats for the day. Either is fine if you don’t care, or if you prefer to mix it up.

There are a few supplements that can help you in your fitness journey, but none of them are necessary. Creatine is one of the best-known muscle-building supplements. It’s understood to be effective, but here’s the thing: Just because it does something for most people doesn’t mean it does very much. If you decide it’s too expensive or just that you would rather not have another thing to remember to take every day, you’re not missing out on any substantial amount of gains.

Likewise, protein powder is a helpful way to get more protein in your diet, but you don’t need to use a supplement; you can just eat more protein-containing foods.

And finally, pre-workout drinks can give you more energy in the gym (it’s mostly caffeine), but the idea that you need it is a very recent development. Even ten years ago, it wasn’t really a thing. People showed up to the gym with a coffee or a coke or with no caffeine at all in their stomach, and worked out just fine.

Look, people have been exercising successfully for millennia, but all of our apps and devices weren't even a thing until the 2000s. Tracking every minute, every step, or every mile of your routine is not actually necessary. You’re still a runner even if you don’t have an app that knows how many miles you ran. You don’t even have to track your sets and reps in your lifting journal if you don’t want to. Your body is what knows how much work you put in, even if your phone were to get wiped overnight.

#3285. Ex-Legora and Big Law lawyers get a16z backing for AI law firm Athena

Two months after launching, Athena has signed 22 clients. Its proprietary AI agents work alongside experienced attorneys to turn complex deal documents around in hours, not weeks.

Athena co-founders Cem Ucan and Kieran John Keenan.

In commercial real estate, speed can make or break a deal. Offers move in hours and capital moves in seconds, yet legal paperwork can still take weeks. Athena is changing that.

The company has raised a $2.5 million pre-seed round led by a16z Speedrun.

Athena’s proprietary AI agents work alongside experienced transactional attorneys at its affiliated law firm. They deliver complex deal documents in hours, at a fraction of the traditional cost. Legal work can finally move at the speed of dealmaking.

Legal AI is booming, but most of it is being sold to firms that still make money by the hour. When AI turns ten hours of work into two, those firms stand to lose revenue.

Athena flips those economics. Athena’s affiliated law firm charges a fixed fee per transaction, typically 30-50% less than clients paid on recent deals. The faster Athena works, the better the economics for both the firm and its clients.

For commercial real estate investors completing 10-15 acquisitions a year, that speed can make a material difference.

“Most legal AI companies sell tools to traditional law firms. We took a different approach,” said Cem Ucan, Co-Founder and CEO of Athena. “Our AI works hand-in-hand with a law firm designed around it from day one, with experienced attorneys focused on the judgment and negotiation that actually move deals forward.”

For clients, working with Athena feels like working with a traditional law firm. They send documents to their attorney and receive legal work back. Behind the scenes, proprietary AI agents handle much of the heavy lifting.

Athena’s affiliated law firm advises on commercial real estate acquisitions, sales and financing. Its work runs from purchase agreements and due diligence to loan documents and closings.

When a new agreement comes in, Athena’s agents review it against the deal terms and identify inconsistencies. They prepare redlines and draft client communications. They also draw on previous transactions to understand each client’s negotiating preferences.

Experienced attorneys review the work, make the legal decisions and approve everything before it reaches the client.

The results are already showing. On an early transaction, the team turned around a purchase agreement in under 48 hours. It was the fastest turnaround the client said they had experienced.

“A lot of firms in our industry have an AI task force in name only,” said L. Miguel Arce, CEO at Mox, a Texas-based multifamily real estate investment, property management, and development company. “What stood out about Athena is that the system learns from every deal, from what the attorneys change to what we prefer. Speed only matters if it’s quality work, and the Athena platform gets us both.”

And the platform gets better with every deal. Attorney corrections and client preferences feed back into the system, reducing the work needed on future transactions. In its first six weeks, Athena cut attorney review time by more than 70%.

“I measure our progress by how quickly an attorney can review an AI agent’s work and confidently stand behind it,” said Kieran John Keenan, Co-Founder and CTO of Athena. “A draft produced in minutes can still leave a lawyer with hours of work. Making that review more efficient is how our platform helps us deliver faster legal services with the quality clients expect from Big Law.”

In commercial real estate, speed can determine who wins a deal. Some Athena clients make several offers a week and submit dozens of offers for every deal they close. Once a property goes under contract, every day counts.

That urgency could soon extend across the market. Many commercial properties acquired in 2021 and 2022 were financed with three-to-five-year loans now approaching maturity.

As refinancing pressure builds, Athena’s founders expect more properties to change hands. That would drive a new wave of transactions and legal work. Athena is positioning itself to handle that volume. It aims to give investors the speed and cost advantages of AI, with experienced attorneys accountable for every deal.

Athena’s founders met at Legora, where they both saw the potential of AI and the limitations of selling it to traditional law firms.

Cem Ucan had spent years in Big Law, at one point billing 3,000 hours annually, before moving into legal innovation at Baker McKenzie and Legora.

Kieran John Keenan studied law before building an automated legal reasoning system at his own startup. It combined legal understanding with hands-on AI engineering and evaluation. As Legora’s founding evaluations engineer, he then built systems to assess and improve AI performance across drafting, research and agentic workflows.

The idea for Athena took shape when Kieran built a prototype that could turn hundreds of documents into a first-draft due diligence report. The founders saw an opportunity to build a new kind of legal service around the technology.

José Braz, who developed Legora’s legal research agent and broader legal research capabilities, joined as founding engineer. Together, Kieran and José built what is now Athena’s own end-to-end deal platform.

Troy Kirwin, partner at a16z Speedrun, said: “As AI becomes more capable, clients will still want experienced professionals who take responsibility for the work. Athena is building around that need, with a system that can improve through real legal work and a team obsessed with scaling fast.”

Commercial real estate is just the beginning. Athena plans to expand across property types, geographies and eventually other areas of transactional law, with an ambition to fundamentally change how quickly business gets done.

“We want legal work to be measured in seconds and minutes rather than weeks and months,” said Ucan. “Our ambition is to free a 21st-century economy from a 19th-century legal delivery model.”

Athena helps commercial real estate investors close deals faster. Its proprietary AI agents work alongside experienced transactional attorneys at its affiliated law firm on acquisitions, sales and financing, from purchase agreements and due diligence to loan documents and closings.

Legal services are provided exclusively by Athena Circle, which offers fixed-fee pricing, with attorneys responsible for every legal decision and all work delivered to clients. Backed by a16z Speedrun, Athena is building a new model for legal services that makes complex transactions faster and more affordable.

#3284. Hands-on: ESR’s 45W Xtend charger is an excellent iPhone fast charger on the go

Last month, ESR released a new set of chargers under the xtend branding – all of which offer built-in retractable cables. They have a 45W wall charger that supports up to 60W with AVS, as well as a 100W car charger with two cables.

I’ll largely be touching on the 45W charger here, as that’s the one I’ve been utilizing the most.

Chargers with built-in retractable cables have been a larger trend in the past year or so, and ESR’s new chargers offer larger cables than usual. On the 45W Xtend charger, you get up to 3.1ft of cable length with the built in cable, compared to other offerings which are around 2.2ft.

I’ve been carrying around ESR’s new 45W charger for the past few weeks since it debuted, and I like it quite a bit. It comes in a few color options: black, white, as well as burgundy to match the iPhone 18 Pro.

You don’t only have to rely on the built-in retractable cable. The charger also offers a normal USB-C port for connecting any cable you’d like, including a longer one.

Personally, I love packing it for travel. Throwing a charging brick and a cable into a bag can be a little cumbersome at times, especially since cables can get tangled. I find chargers with retractable cables quite refreshing since they’re much easier to deal with in a pinch.

45W alone is plenty for fast charging any iPhone, but it also supports up to 60W dynamic charging with AVS, which’ll unlock the fastest charge speeds on iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max.

ESR’s 45W xtend charger is normally available for $49.99, though right now it’s on sale for as low as $35.99 on Amazon in the white colorway. Burgundy is also available for $41.99, saving you 20%.

Their 100W car charger also offers two retractable cables, as well as an extra USB-A port. I don’t have many thoughts to offer on the car charger as I don’t drive, but I would imagine it’s nice to not have to deal with cables in your center console area. With 100W, you can fast charge pretty much any iPhone, iPad, MacBook Air, or base 14-inch MacBook Pro. It’s available for just $36.99 on Amazon right now, a $20 discount.

The tale of a successful legal aid Diana McGowin (Mia Farrow), the businesswoman’s life gradually begins to unravel after she starts suffering from confusion and short-term memory loss. As she’s the main breadwinner in her family, Diana decides to keep her illness from her husband Jack (a predictably charming Martin Sheen) and the rest of her family. Up until the launch of MacBook Neo, the MacBook Air represented the entry point to Apple’s laptop lineup. Despite MacBook Neo making its value proposition slightly questionable, I’d still say MacBook Air is a great laptop if you want a better experience without needing anything premium.

MagSafe, a P3 color display, Center Stage on the webcam, and more battery life are just a few of the highlights with MacBook Air. It also comes with a 15-inch size variant, unlike MacBook Neo which only offers 13-inch.

Right now, you can find these discounts across the MacBook Air lineup:

This product doesn’t need a long explanation – MacBook Neo is Apple’s first affordable MacBook, coming in at just $699.

It has some compromises compared to the aforementioned MacBook Air, but it’s still incredibly good for the price. Build quality, display sharpness, and the macOS experience are all essentially uncompromised. Sure, you have to deal with a slower A18 Pro chip (though trust me, it’s no slouch), lesser ports, and 8GB of memory, but it’s perfectly reasonable for the price. It also comes in fun colors like Citrus, Blush, and Indigo.

There’s no notable retail discounts on MacBook Neo right now, though Apple does offer them refurbished for $100-120 off compared to retail pricing. Apple refurbished offers the same 1 year warranty and a like-new experience, with every major component being replaced. You won’t find any scuffs nor battery degradation.

Apple just debuted its revamped MacBook Pro models with PROLED XDR displays and touchscreens. They come in at higher prices, and the older miniLED-based M5 Pro and M5 Max models still remain in the lineup. At the same time, the company also introduced a refreshed base model 14-inch MacBook Pro with the M6 chip. For now, M5 models remain available at a discount.

#3281. Samsung to make AMD and Nvidia HBM parts at second Texas fab, report says

Maeil Business says the 2nm Taylor plant is fully booked before its construction formally starts this month.

Samsung will use its second chip plant in Taylor, Texas, to make parts for AMD and Nvidia’s AI memory, South Korea’s Maeil Business Newspaper reported on Tuesday, citing industry sources.

The plant will produce base dies for high-bandwidth memory, the logic layer that sits at the bottom of the stacked memory chips feeding AI processors. Most of the booked volume is for AMD, per the report. The paper says the plant has already secured orders for its entire output.

Samsung declined to comment, and Reuters said it could not confirm the report. TNW has not independently verified it either.

The second Taylor fab will run on Samsung’s advanced 2-nanometre process and cover about 2.7 million square feet, roughly 1.5 times the size of the first plant, per the report. Formal construction is due to start this month. Equipment should arrive from February 2029, with mass production in 2030.

The first Taylor plant, a project that grew from $17 billion to a $37 billion total investment, is due to start mass production in 2027. Its anchor customer is Tesla, which signed a $16.5 billion contract for its AI5 and AI6 chips. The 1,268-acre site has room for up to 10 fabs.

The project has been visible on the ground for months. Taylor’s city council approved engineering support for the second fab’s permits back in March, and Samsung has been hiring for the campus. The first plant’s bill includes a $4.75 billion subsidy under the US CHIPS Act.

A second fab filled before ground is broken would mark a turnaround for Samsung’s foundry arm, which has lost money for years.

Kiwoom Securities expects the unit to return to profit from the fourth quarter. Samsung has projected that its 2nm orders will grow more than 130% this year, helped by AI demand and strained capacity at rival TSMC.

It would also deepen the US supply chain for AI memory, where demand has outrun supply. Memory rivals are racing to catch up, from SK Hynix to China’s CXMT. AMD, meanwhile, has been locking in capacity across the board as its AI chip business scales up.

#3278. AI apps with hidden sexual and violent deepfake features made it into the App Store

Hundreds of AI apps with hidden sexual and violent deepfake features made it into Apple’s App Store after passing app review. The same apps were also available in the Google Play Store.

An investigation discovered more than 400 apps, apparently created by a single Chinese organization. The apps allow users to upload photos and then generate sexual and violent deepfakes which could be used to humiliate or threaten victims …

A Wired investigation discovered a network of more than 400 connected domains and apps with hidden abusive functionality.

Apps like Viefur [ostentibly used to add clothing to pet photos] often claim to be everyday services—such as language tuition or AI workout coaches. When accessed under certain conditions, however, apps in the network stealthily load a web interface allowing the generation of explicit AI sexual images and videos using photos users upload. The apps include AI scenes such as “bedroom rape” and “threatening knife,” where a man holds a knife to a woman’s neck.

I feel like this going to be a never ending cat and mouse game. Much like Apple has always had with jailbreaks.

Wired says that the network is “hiding in plain sight,” thanks to thousands of video ads for them published on Facebook and Instagram. Some of the apps have been around for a year and have passed review by Apple, Google, and Meta despite each having clear policies prohibiting harmful deepfake content.

Bait-and-switch tactics were used to pass app review. The apps normally show benign content, but a server check can activate the hidden features. Downloading the app after tapping an ad for the deepfake functionality on Meta platforms appears to be one of the triggers. Dozens of pornography photo and video templates can then be downloaded, with credits purchased to generate deepfakes from user-uploaded photos.

Apple removed 19 apps after Wired shared details.

We review every app before it’s published, and these apps complied with our rules when we reviewed them. After approval, their developers changed the website the app pulls its content from, replacing what we approved with pornographic content, and promoted it through pornographic ads hosted on a third-party platform.

The company recently strengthened protections against this approach. Meta says it has taken action against more than 10,000 ad accounts linked to domains associated with these apps.

#3277. The Robot I Didn’t Expect to Build

The November issue of IEEE Spectrum is here!

Agility Robotics’ first practical robotic worker is nothing like I dreamed

Author and Agility Robotics co-founder Jonathan Hurst next to his new Digit 5 humanoid robot worker.

Agility Robotics, the company I cofounded out of my robotics lab at Oregon State University in 2015, has just launched Digit 5. It’s designed to be the first humanoid robot that can safely and economically do useful work at scale, allowing us to bring tens of thousands of humanoid workers into the real world. Engineered to lift 23-kilogram bins onto high shelves and with a battery that can run for 90 minutes on a 9-minute charge, Digit 5’s goal is to handle heavy warehouse tasks shift after shift, filling the need for labor in jobs that are too physically stressful or too dull for humans to want to do.

Digit 5 is what Agility has been working toward for over a decade. But the robot is heavy and bulky, lacking the graceful natural motion of its predecessors, and it’s farther than I thought possible from the robot I dreamed of building when I started this company. To deliver a useful commercial product, Agility has taken a path that is very different from what I first imagined.

My dream has always been to build robots that combine locomotion and manipulation to move through the world and interact with it as people do. I seek a mastery of motion, achieved through devices designed to navigate the constraints of physics with elegance. When I started the Dynamic Robotics Laboratory at Oregon State in 2008, we began with a theory derived from decades of work in biomechanics: that a simple “spring-mass” model (a body supported by legs that act like springs) should be able to reproduce every known walking and running gait found in animals.

We put theory into practice by building the bipedal robot ATRIAS—short for “Assume The Robot Is A Sphere,” a joke among physicists about reducing a complex system to its simplest possible form. ATRIAS looked like a large microwave on stilts because it was only intended to demonstrate the physics of human walking and running. This was the first glimmer of achieving my dream; even though ATRIAS wasn’t designed to look like us, it still seemed natural, and even somehow alive, when it settled into a walking gait.

With the success of ATRIAS, the barriers to progress shifted from scientific to engineering and organizational, and a startup company seemed like the way to bridge the gap from a one-off research concept to an actual robotic product. I felt confident of two things: that I would be able to build robots that could go where people go, and that this capability would be incredibly useful. This combination of ambition and naivete is necessary for anyone to found a new company—how hard could it be?

Good advice for starting a company is to understand a customer problem, and then find a way to solve it using your unique capabilities. My cofounders, Damion Shelton and Mikhail Jones, and I did not do this. We relied on our belief that this technology would enable new possibilities and trusted ourselves to figure out the business as we went. So we simply focused on building our first product: the bipedal robot Cassie.

Cassie was the first dynamic bipedal robot that researchers could buy, able to maintain its balance through active, fluid motion rather than careful, rigid steps. It had ostrichlike legs, not because we were imitating ground-running birds, but as a result of engineering strictly for performance. It was not intended to be commercially useful, and had no torso, arms, or head. We sold Cassie robots to Harvard, Caltech, the University of Michigan, the University of California, Berkeley, and a handful of other research institutions, ultimately saturating the market for US $250,000 bipedal research robots after having sold a total of 10 of them.

ATRIAS, Cassie, and Digit 4 EVT [left to right] are on display at Agility Robotics’ RoboFab in Salem, Ore. The 70,000-square-foot facility has the capacity to produce more than 10,000 Digit 5 robots per year.Agility Robotics

Because Cassie’s hardware enabled research into the physics of walking and running, the legged-robot research frontier shifted to control software. Traditionally, engineers controlled legged robots with detailed mathematical models that determined how the machines should move. With Cassie, researchers pioneered the new approach of reinforcement learning for bipedal legged locomotion: A simulated robot learns through trial and error, and the resulting neural network controls the physical machine. This approach is what enables virtually all of the dynamic behaviors that you see on legged robots today, and Cassie looked alive as it recovered from stumbles while climbing stairs, ran 5 kilometers across the Oregon State campus, and broke the robot world record for a 100-meter dash.

Cassie got us closer to being able to move through the world with confidence and grace, but to make it useful, we needed manipulation. After exhaustively exploring different configurations, we found that an upright torso helped the robot balance, while two arms mounted near the top of the torso allowed it to pick up large objects and to catch itself when it fell. Digit 1, which added a torso and arms to the Cassie legs, was our first mobile manipulation robot, and another step on the path toward a product that could do useful work for commercial customers.

As we explored the first applications for Digit, potential customers kept asking us: Why legs? And why a humanoid? These were tough questions for me to answer, because they exposed a core business reality: It didn’t matter to Agility Robotics if we solved a cool science problem in a beautiful way. What mattered to the business was solving real problems for customers.

After years of engagement with industry partners, we found one answer in warehouses and manufacturing facilities: moving bins. Bin handling is a clearly defined task where two arms are needed to lift large bins up high and legs are the best way to balance and move in narrow spaces. Because the task can vary widely from one deployment to another, it hasn’t been broadly addressed by single-purpose automation. Yet it was constrained enough to give Digit an economically viable first job while it developed a broader set of skills.

In 2019, Digit began demonstrating its capabilities to do real work. With Ford Motor Company, we showed how Digit 1 could carry packages from an autonomous vehicle to a front porch. We developed Digit 2 and 3 while working with a certain global package delivery company on moving and sorting cardboard boxes. Amazon tested Digit 4 on moving and stacking bins, and it became the world’s first commercially deployed humanoid at the logistics provider GXO. In 2024, Digit appeared on the cover of Time magazine.

Despite Digit’s apparent success, we began to run into conflicts between my dream and the needs of actual customers. We were no longer working with relatively patient university research labs. Agility has to sell robots to survive, and customers will only purchase robots that provide value. If bins weren’t moving, our customers were losing money. We spent a huge amount of time and effort keeping our first deployments operational, which arguably eliminated any profit we made. Yet this also kept our company learning and alive the way no lab demo ever could.

I had no idea how hard it would be, or that running a company would involve so many things that have nothing to do with solving technical problems: deployments across the country; shipping, service, and customer support; fundraising and investor relations; more fundraising; human resources and IT; developing fleet-management software; managing a supply chain; and even more fundraising. I had no experience with any of these things. My career had focused on solving the technical challenges of robots interacting with the world, and it turned out that was only a tiny piece of building a successful robotics company. But Agility was the only path I saw to continuing the technical work and having an impact.

I knew that Agility needed to focus more on robots as a product, but I didn’t know how to make that happen. Hiring the people we needed to run the company meant giving up an immense amount of control, but we had no other choice. We recruited a new executive team with the experience required to commercialize this new technology, and they quickly made changes that were both painful and necessary.

Digit versions 1, 2, and 3 [left to right] show the evolution of the robot from a dynamic walking platform into a useful mobile manipulator. Agility

We had intended the next revision of Digit, Digit 4 EVT (Engineering Validation and Test), to be a relatively minor upgrade. But Agility’s new leadership insisted that the robot was missing key features that were essential if Digit was going to become a real product. So Digit 4 EVT instead incorporated a series of major changes in a highly compressed timeline, such as larger batteries and system-wide upgrades for safety and regulatory compliance, which added enough mass to dramatically alter the robot’s appearance and capabilities.

While early Digits were headless, Agility Robotics was able to justify a head for Digit 4 to optimize antenna and camera placement, and it turned out to be surprisingly useful for human-robot interaction.Christie Hemm Klok

I could only watch as others brought their own talents to bear to make Digit into a successful product, in gut-wrenching ways that didn’t always align with my vision. There were some especially difficult times when I felt like there were compromises made that didn’t seem necessary, but making those decisions was no longer my sole responsibility. I had to accept that Digit had grown far beyond me, and look for ways of influencing decisions rather than directing them. In the moment, it was incredibly frustrating, as Digit 4 EVT took a few steps backward from my vision of how humanoids should look and move.

Agility is in our name because agility is core to the future of the company. I want Digit to be lithe and graceful. When people see Digit, I want them to like the robot, to understand what it can do at a glance, and to feel that it’s there to help. But with Digit 4 EVT, all of that was sacrificed to functionality, because of course it had to be—the customer just needs the robot to do the work. The design process became a ruthless triage, with aesthetics and elegance of movement being delayed over and over again in favor of brutal functionality. For an engineer whose mind lives more in the future than in the present, it has been hard for me to accept this trajectory. And yet, through Digit 4 EVT’s commercial deployments, we began to really understand specific applications and what they required. We mapped the first 10 use cases Digit would perform, and then began designing Digit 5 from scratch based on everything we had learned.

Digit 5 will be Agility’s first real step toward a general-purpose robot. It marks our transition from imagining what a future humanoid robot should be to designing a product around the realities of customer deployments. These realities include things like European CE regulatory compliance, North American UL electrical-safety certifications, and Federal Communications Commission limits for electromagnetic radiation—all of which felt tangential to my dream for Digit, but were absolute requirements.

Digit 5 is designed to be the first humanoid robot that can operate safely next to human coworkers while working 20 hours a day and lifting more than a human can.Christie Hemm Klok

Customer requirements helped us realize that safety in particular was one of the most critical barriers to scaling. In Digit 4’s commercial deployments, the robots had to work behind physical barriers, separated from humans at all times, to meet insurance and regulatory demands. This seemed silly to me, because I’ve never felt that our robots were dangerous, but we have to prove that they’re safe. And since keeping the robots in safety cages severely limited their usefulness, enabling Digit 5 to operate safely around people became a primary design goal. We spent two years on this challenge.

Digit 5 is designed to be the first humanoid robot that can operate safely next to human coworkers. It will rely on an array of sensors to locate nearby people in a manner that’s certifiably safe, and then take actions based on that information. As a person approaches, Digit 5 is programmed to stop what it’s doing, set down its payload, sit on the floor, and cut power to its motors before the person gets close enough to touch the robot. This conservative approach reduces the risk to nearby people in a verifiable way, and we believe it’s the only approach that makes sense as a first step toward working alongside humans.

Yet this strategy also feels like a massive slowdown on the path toward robots becoming part of everyday life. Enabling coexistence with humans has influenced almost every aspect of Digit 5’s design: the shape of the legs and the body, the safety-rated sensors within protective housings, the isolated computers dedicated to safety, and more. All of these features increase the robot’s complexity, power consumption, mass, and physical size.

Digit 5 is Agility’s largest, heaviest, strongest, and most capable humanoid robot worker.

The robot’s design was driven by safety, with integrated protection for the robot and for the humans it will work around.Agility Robotics

Weighing over 120 kg, Digit 5 is a huge robot. It needed to achieve the lifting limits recommended under the U.S. National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health guidelines for human workers, which include repeatedly lifting 23-kg bins and reaching shelves 1.75 meters high. Digit is designed to perform tasks like these for 20 hours a day—something no human can do. This requires motors with enough power and torque to lift the load, but also enough precision to delicately control the force Digit applies when it makes contact with the world. To power those motors, we needed a large battery and a dock for rapid autonomous charging. The dock will deliver 240 amperes at 48 volts, which is enough current to make its thick charging cables visibly wiggle under the induced magnetic forces, while powerful fans blow air through cooling channels in the robot’s torso to keep the battery from overheating. The battery and cooling system takes up about 75 percent of Digit’s torso, but it will allow the robot to operate for 90 minutes and fully recharge during a 9-minute break, enabling near-continuous work.

All of this extra bulk means that Digit 5 can no longer run or jump the way previous generations could, and the svelte form I imagined has become physically impossible. In some ways, Digit 5 feels more like a forklift than the graceful humanoid I set out to build. But looking at the situation rationally, I believe this trade-off is necessary for any company that claims its humanoid can do this kind of work today: If you see a robot that looks like a human working in a factory or warehouse, it either can’t lift the required weight or can’t make it through the whole shift. And if it’s not covered with sensors, it’s likely not safe to stand next to.

The most visible change with Digit 5 is that humanlike legs replace the ostrichlike legs of our earlier versions. While the “backward” leg configuration was optimized for walking and running, we discovered that it created problems with squatting because the ankle will strike the ground. Digit 5 will spend a lot of time lifting heavy objects from near the floor, so we used a humanoid leg configuration with knee and hip motors that both contribute torque to help the robot stand up again.

When Digit detects an approaching human, the robot will lower itself to the floor and cut power to its motors. Agility believes this is the only near-term approach to verifiably reduce risk when the robot is working near people.Agility Robotics

Other companies building humanoid robots have copied the human form without ever understanding its purpose. It’s very frustrating that, to an outside observer, it now looks like we discarded Agility’s distinctive leg design and simply did what everyone else was doing. Yet I know that we arrived at this shape based purely on functional engineering choices. Making a robot look like a human is the easy part—without the function to match, and the understanding of the physics underlying that function, the whole point of the human form may be lost.

With the power, battery life, and safety features that we are designing into Digit 5, we will have a truly useful robot. But it also compromises on some things that are core to my vision and mission. I understand why we made the choices we did and can justify them all, but together they leave me unsatisfied. It’s the curse of the engineer.

I believe Digit 5 will be the scaling moment for Agility Robotics, the inflection point where we can begin deploying robots in large numbers. While the robot will continue carrying bins, our road map includes many more tasks, from picking individual items and tending machines, to preparing parts for assembly and shipping, and eventually doing assembly work itself. Its interchangeable tool interfaces and modular design will enable us to gradually upgrade its subsystems. It will be a platform for improvement, a source of data for future behavior training, and a viable product all at the same time.

Hurst stands between the previous version of Digit, Digit 4 [left], and Digit 5.Christie Hemm Klok

But I cannot love Digit 5. It’s the largest, heaviest, most expensive robot Agility will ever build, full of design compromises that enable it to be exactly the robot it needs to be right now rather than the robot I dreamed of. In the beginning, I envisioned steady progress on agility and dexterity, with each version becoming more dynamically capable. Instead, developing Digit 5 has required large detours to incorporate requirements that seemed unrelated to my original vision. However, I now recognize that tackling these challenges was always necessary. Customers and product requirements didn’t ruin my vision; they revealed what my vision was missing. This is how robots will achieve commercial success and make a real-world impact, which will bring me closer to my scientific dream as well.

We won’t have a humanoid that matches the capabilities of humans until it achieves that mastery of motion that inspired me to found Agility over a decade ago. I saw glimmers of it with the spring-mass locomotion of ATRIAS, and more glimmers with Cassie’s running gait.

I know that such mastery is physically possible with the tools and hardware that we have right now, and despite all of its compromises, Digit 5 will give us a practical foundation for pursuing that dream. I want every future version of Digit to be lighter and more graceful, to interact more naturally with humans, and to be better at manipulating objects and moving through the world, enabling robots to enter aspects of our lives that they haven’t been able to help with before. By the time I’m old enough to need assistance at home, I expect Digit will be up to the task.

With Digit 5, Agility has built a robot that will be useful in our world. Now I’m getting back to work to make it beautiful, too.

This article appears in the November 2026 print issue.

Jonathan W. Hurst is the co-founder and chief robot officer of Agility Robotics and a robotics professor at Oregon State University.

Why humanoid though? In particular, why bi-pedal? Why use legs at all? Are wheels surely better and easier? Legs seem like unnecessary complexity. Wheels on 'legs" for suspension can be a great alternative. I don't understand the obsession with humanoid form?

This is the most honest account I've read from a robotics founder. While Tesla and Figure are still showing demos, Agility has actually deployed robots in real customer environments, moved over 100,000 totes at GXO, and hit 98% accuracy at Schaeffler. Digit 5's specs are driven entirely by what customers need: 20 hours of work per day, 9-minute charge, 23 kg lift to 1.75 m shelves. That's real engineering for real problems. The tension between engineering vision and commercial reality is something every robotics founder will face. Professor Hurst lays it out without spin.

It seems to me that even at scale production, the robot we employ in industry should do jobs people cannot. Highly radioactive, highly toxic, and factors where the atmosphere needs to be unsuitable for humans. i.e., oxygen-deprived environment or low pressure/vacuum. Or use them on the 3rd shift when people are less willing to work.

Robots should increase manufacturing that was impossible to do in the past. We should be exploring new types of manufacturing, not replacing people in manufacturing that humans can do. That's how you create growth.
