#3274. Affinity for iPad all-in-one design app now available, free for individuals

Design app Affinity has long been popular with Mac users, and a long-awaited iPad version has launched today. Canva promises that Affinity for iPad offers “the same pro-level power” as the Mac app.

It’s been a year since the company’s vector, photo, and layout tools were unified into a single app on Mac, and the same is now true on iPad …

Created specifically for the touch-first interface and unique capabilities of iPad and Apple Pencil, the app brings professional sketch, vector, photo and layout editing together with the same pro-level power of Affinity on the desktop […]

With Affinity for iPad, creatives can take a project from first sketch with Apple Pencil to print-ready file on iPad alone. And it’s free for individuals, just like Affinity on desktop, which has recorded more than seven million sign-ups since launching a year ago.

“Creative work doesn’t stay in one discipline, so your tools shouldn’t either,” said Duncan Clark, CEO of Pro Design at Canva. “Since we brought Affinity together on desktop, our biggest user request has been the desire to bring it to iPad. Today we’re delivering it: a fully-fledged, professional app built for touch.”

Being able to carry out all of the work within a single app on a single file is a key attraction of Affinity. The integrated app replaces the separate Affinity Photo, Affinity Publisher, and Affinity Designer apps.

Sketch: Rough out concepts the moment they land, with the unique capabilities of Apple Pencil like pressure and tilt in every mark, thick where you press and soft where you tilt. A full brush library comes with controls to shape each brush into the exact tool you need. Sketches stay live in the file to build on, rather than trace again.

Vector: Responsive, smooth and under control. Build a full logo or icon system with real curves and precise nodes, or bring a rough drawing through from Sketch. Sketch to Shapes turns hand-drawn forms into clean vector shapes.

Photo: Fine-tune RAW files, make intelligent selections, retouch in real time and build full composites at the shoot or on the go. Users can even sketch over a photo first to plan where a subject or prop should sit. The Mask Tool finds the boundary as the Apple Pencil pixel precision runs along a challenging edge, so hair, fur and foliage take a stroke rather than an afternoon. Every mask, grade and retouch stays live and undoable, even thousands of layers deep.

Layout: Create multi-page documents such as ‘zines, lookbooks and photo books, with text and images flowing across pages; master pages and grids keep everything consistent, and typography exactly right. Projects go all the way to a print-ready file with proper colour handling.

Canva says the app supports all of the advanced capabilities of Apple Pencil Pro: pressure, tilt, barrel roll, squeeze, and hover. AI features include generative expand, upscaling resolution, and adding attributes like motion blur. A Decompose Layer feature even splits a flat image into editable layers.

Affinity for iPad is a free download from the App Store.

#3273. Fourthline and Veridas complete merger to fight AI identity fraud

Finch Capital, Seaya Andromeda and Ashgrove Capital are providing up to €65m for the Fourthline deal. The combined company expects more than €50m in revenue in 2026.

Fourthline chief executive Paul Stoddart will run the identity verification group formed by his company’s merger with Spain’s Veridas, which closed on Tuesday. The two companies first announced the deal on 16 July.

The combined company checks the identities of customers for banks and other regulated businesses. It handles know-your-customer (KYC) and anti-money laundering checks, biometrics and fraud prevention, and says it works in more than 50 countries. It is on track for 200 million verifications in 2026, according to the announcements by Fourthline and Veridas.

“Closing marks the establishment of a true European Leader in identity and fraud prevention. Starting today, a business partner onboarding customers in Amsterdam, Madrid, London, Mexico City, São Paulo or Bogotá will be able to apply a single verification standard through a single provider,” said Stoddart.

The deal comes with up to €65m in funding. Existing shareholder Finch Capital is providing part of it. Seaya Andromeda is making a new equity investment, and Ashgrove Capital is supplying debt financing. The announcement does not say how the total is split.

The money will go to product development, acquisitions and refinancing debt. It also funds a reorganisation of the shareholdings, which includes partial liquidity for Veridas shareholders.

The companies project combined revenue of more than €50m in 2026. Both were EBITDA-positive at closing, they said, and they expect to reach €85m in annual recurring revenue in 2029.

They also expect €20m a year in run-rate synergies. Their customers overlap little, so most of that growth is meant to come from selling each company’s technology to the other’s clients.

Eduardo Azanza, Veridas’s co-founder and chief executive, becomes president of the combined company. Radboud Vlaar, managing partner at Finch Capital, chairs the supervisory board. The headquarters will be in Amsterdam, with offices in Stockholm, Pamplona, Barcelona, Mexico, São Paulo and Boston.

Fourthline was founded in Amsterdam in 2017. Its clients include Revolut, N26, Trade Republic, Qonto, Rabobank and Bitpanda. Veridas was founded the same year as a joint venture with the Spanish bank BBVA. It says it serves more than 350 clients in 25 countries.

“Our mission is clear: we tell the real from the fake, so our customers can build on trust. This merger gives us the talent, technology and reach to take that mission further than either company could alone,” said Azanza.

The companies say regulated businesses face two pressures at once. Fraud is more and more generated by AI, including deepfakes and synthetic identities. At the same time, compliance rules are widening.

Those rules include the EU’s anti-money laundering rules (AMLR), the MiCA crypto rules, eIDAS 2.0 and national age verification laws. In Mexico and Latin America, they also include rules from regulators such as Mexico’s banking supervisor, the CNBV.

The companies cite Juniper Research, which expects global spending on digital identity verification to reach nearly $19bn in 2026. It forecasts growth of 55% to more than $29bn by 2030.

Customers of either company keep their existing contracts, integrations and support. The two platforms will be integrated in phases, and the companies say customers do not need to take any action.

The November issue of IEEE Spectrum is here!

They include humanitarian initiatives and STEM education programs

Kathy Pretz is the editor in chief of The Institute, IEEE's member publication

IEEE MOVE, EPICS in IEEE, the IEEE Global Museum, and the TryEngineering Summer Institute, were some of the projects showcased in the 2025 Social Impact Report.

Advancing technology for the benefit of humanity isn’t just the tagline for IEEE’s mission as a public charity. It’s something that the organization’s more than 500,000 members strive to do all the time. IEEE’s recently released 2025 Social Impact Report showcases a variety of programs volunteers worked on to increase public awareness of technology’s impact on society, many of which The Institute covered.

Here is a selection of the programs from the report, with links to our related articles:

“The IEEE global community of more than 500,000 members and volunteers demonstrates what is possible when expertise is mobilized for the public good,” Sophia Muirhead, IEEE executive director and chief operating officer, said in a news release about the Social Impact Report. “Technology has the power to expand opportunity, strengthen communities and improve lives, and IEEE’s mission is to ensure that this power is used responsibly, ethically, and in service of humanity. The 2025 report shows how IEEE members and volunteers are advancing solutions that make a real difference in people’s lives around the world.”

Engagement research shows that members increasingly cited “giving back to my profession and the world community” as a reason for joining IEEE and renewing their membership, IEEE President Mary Ellen Randall said in her September column about the report.

“Humanitarian programs are not only meaningful,” she wrote. “They also are magnetic. They attract younger engineers, keep them engaged, and help them build a professional identity rooted in purpose and impact.

“IEEE has the opportunity to become the world’s leading convening force for developing interdisciplinary technology solutions to solve humanity’s most important challenges. Our future relevance will be defined not only by the technologies we advance but also by the problems we choose to help solve.”

#3271. Here’s everything new Apple TV has coming in November

Apple TV’s November lineup includes the return of a beloved comedy, a heist thriller with big stars, the follow-up film to its Oscar winner, and a lot more. Here’s everything new coming to Apple TV in November.

“Stick” is a sports comedy series created by Jason Keller and starring and executive produced by Owen Wilson. Wilson stars as Pryce Cahill, an over-the-hill, ex-pro golfer whose career was derailed prematurely 20 years ago. After the collapse of his marriage and while working at an Indiana sporting goods store, Pryce hedges his bets, and future, entirely on a troubled 17-year-old golf phenom named Santi (Peter Dager). “Stick” is a heartfelt, feel-good comedy about a found family and their relationships set within the world of golf as it has never been shown before.

Hollywood actor and comedian Nora Lum (aka Awkwafina) is the descendant of restaurant royalty … but she can’t cook. Join the star on an inspiring culinary road trip as she learns the craft and attempts to revive her family’s beloved Chinese eatery.

Each episode of “12 12 12” unfolds across three timelines of a heist: the 12 months of planning, the 12 hours of the heist and the 12 days following it. The series follows a disgraced FBI agent (Anthony Mackie) and an American career criminal (Jamie Dornan) as they play a zero-sum game of cat and mouse across Europe. At the center of it all is the daring, epic raid on a bank vault deep beneath the streets of Zurich.

They wouldn’t take Judy Heumann’s phone calls, so she took their building. In 1977, a young disabled woman (Ruth Madeley) and a scrappy coalition of outsiders decide they’ve had enough. What begins as one impulsive act becomes the longest occupation of a federal building in American history, as hundreds spontaneously seize government offices and refuse to leave until the bureaucrat in their way (Mark Ruffalo) takes action. Bringing rebellion in all its forms to the hallowed halls, a movement’s accidental leaders struggle to find their path forward where none has ever been paved for them. Directed by Academy Award winner Siân Heder (“CODA”) and based on true events, “Being Heumann” is the revolutionary, irreverent and deeply human story of the least likely people trying to pull off the impossible and change the lives of millions.

In the latest special under the acclaimed “Snoopy Presents” banner, the Peanuts kids are on their best behavior — but Snoopy has landed on Santa’s naughty list. With just 12 days until Christmas, he sets out to prove he’s not such a bad beagle after all, discovering along the way that the season is about more than gifts.

Middle school has been a nightmare for Marc (Jude Hill), a good kid who’s bullied by his classmates and feels like he’s behind in everything, from academics to P.E. to just making friends. That changes when his injured Uncle Jake (Chris Pratt), a decorated Navy SEAL, comes to spend the summer and recuperate with Marc and his mom, Sarah (Linda Cardellini). To help Marc defend himself, Jake devises an ambitious program he calls “Operation Warrior Kid” based on his SEAL training. Instead of teaching his nephew how to fight, Jake shows Marc what real courage is, facing down his own demons along the way. Based on the bestselling novel by former Navy SEAL Jocko Willink, “Way of the Warrior Kid” is directed by McG (“Charlie’s Angels,” “Terminator Salvation”) from a screenplay by Will Staples (“Without Remorse,” “The Right Stuff”).

The TDM. Neo has a hybrid design, giving you a pair of headphones and a portable Bluetooth speaker in one. It’s great for light travel, complemented by impressive battery life and customizable app EQ settings. However, the steep price doesn't quite match the quality; speaker volume is limited, and getting the best sound requires careful balancing.

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

Best for: Anyone short on space when travelling

What if you didn’t have to decide between the best headphones or the best Bluetooth speaker when you’re packing? That’s what the TDM. Neo promises with its hybrid design. This device is creating quite the buzz right now. With Jimmy Fallon declaring it “legendary,” and a decent haul of awards at CES 2026, there’s a reason it turns heads.

The innovative design twists the headphones into a Bluetooth speaker, and it features impressive battery life. With the right EQ settings through the companion app, the sound quality can be pretty good too.

However, the price tag is a little steep, the volume is far too quiet, and getting the best positioning for the speaker takes some time. To find out more about the device, keep reading my full TDM. Neo review.

The TDM. Neo is an interesting device, and there’s a lot to like. The design is a major talking point here, and for good reason — it’s innovative and very useful. The battery life is very impressive, with up to 200 hours of listening in the headphones configuration, and the companion app makes the sound experience even better.

There’s no denying the design of the TDM. Neo turns heads. The headphones transform into a speaker with a simple twist of the headband. They connect with magnets on the side of the headphones so the speaker holds its shape. To listen to your music with headphones instead, you simply unravel the headphones, and the music mode automatically switches. The device weighs 12 ounces, comfortable enough to wear as headphones and to carry around with you as a speaker.

If you’re pushed for space when packing for a trip, I think the TDM. Neo is the perfect solution. When I’m heading on vacation, I always like to have a speaker with me for my room and a set of headphones for travel, and when trying to pack light, this can prove to be somewhat challenging. I honestly thought this would be just another gimmick, but this headphone/speaker combination is one of the most handy gadgets I’ve ever used.

What’s more impressive than the design is the battery life. If you’re using the TDM. Neo as headphones, you’ll get 200 hours of battery life, and if using it as a speaker, you’ll get 16 hours. Obviously, this is a little trickier to put to the test, as I was switching between the modes regularly while using them.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Other headphones in this price range, such as the Sony WH-1000XM5, will give you up to 40 hours of listening. The Marshall Milton ANC headphones cost $229 and have upt ot 80 hours of battery life with ANC turned off, so you can find headphones with much higher listening times, meaning the headphones time of the DM. Neo isn’t that impressive, but the speaker time certainly is.

There is a quick charge option to get eight hours of music playback from five minutes of charge. However, it’s not specified whether this is for the headphones or the speaker mode. The battery module is also replaceable, meaning you’re less likely to have to replace the full unit down the line.

Is this the best sound quality of any headphones or speaker I’ve used? Absolutely not. However, the TDM. Neo’s companion app lets you adjust the EQ settings to make the sound much more balanced. To use the custom EQ feature, you need to create an account, or you can choose from one of the six pre-programmed EQs. I used Qobuz, our pick for the best music streaming service for audiophiles, to listen to music with the speaker and headphones.

During my testing, I created an EQ with increased bass and decreased treble. The high-frequency sounds were a bit tinny, so decreasing the treble made the sound much better. I listened to “Roman Holiday” by Fontaines D.C., which is a guitar-heavy track. It generally sounded good, but even with adjustments, the treble sounded a little tinny and clipped. This is fine for casual listening but makes the soundstage feel narrow. But the bass in this song was impressive and guided the rhythm of the track.

I also listened to “If I Get High” by Nothing But Thieves. This track starts off stripped back and slow, with the vocals as the focus. The vocals sounded amazing and clear here, but as the song built, we were met with the tininess again as the drums and cymbals kicked in. Again, the bass guitar shone here, making the sound much fuller.

Finally, I listened to “Witches” by Alice Phoebe Lou, which features shimmering sounds that carried very well, and actually avoided any tinny sounds at all. The vocals here are very delicate, but they were replicated well through the speaker.

I found the sound quality much better as a speaker when the device is in the carry case, as this acts as sound dampening, so the higher frequencies don’t sound as harsh.

Although I mostly like the TDM. Neo, and I love how innovative the design is, there are a few things that are a little annoying. The price tag seems steep; it doesn’t get loud enough, and it needs that Goldilocks positioning to get the sound just right.

The first thing I don’t like about this device is the price tag. The TDM. Neo is available for $249 /£249 from the TDM. online store, but for this price, I would expect premium sound and build, which I don’t feel I got. The sound is certainly good, but is it $250-good? I don’t think so. Instead, you’re getting a budget pair of headphones and a budget speaker but paying for both devices — you’re paying for the convenience of a two-in-one product.

In terms of quality, I’d liken the speaker to cheaper options like the Tozo PE1, which costs $39. But for around the same price as the TDM. you could get the JBL Charge 6 ($199) that has 28 hours of battery life and louder volume.

If you consider headphones, $249 places you firmly in the premium category. The Marshall Milton headphones cost $229 and have a powerful bass performance, so if the headphones feature on the Neos is what you’ll use most, you should get the Miltons.

The TDM. Neo doesn’t actually get very loud in headphones or speaker mode. When I’m using a speaker, I want to blast my music throughout my whole house, but the sound just doesn't carry.

For massive sound from a small speaker, I’d recommend the Bose SoundLink Micro 2 ($129). This speaker has sound that carries easily and bass that booms when you need it to.

How good the TDM. Neo sounds is highly dependent on its positioning. This is the case for a lot of speakers, but with the twisting nature of the Neo, it’s more important to make sure it’s sat just right. The sound comes from two speakers on either side of where the headphone earcups are folded, so it can’t be placed flat on the table — although this feels most natural. Instead, it needs to be balanced on its side so both speakers are exposed.

This balancing act can feel precarious at times, but with the carry case for the speaker to sit in, you can clip it to something so it’s not touching any surfaces. This is how you’ll get the best sound.

Though I’ve made comparisons to other headphones and speakers throughout this review, it’s not exactly a fair competition. The TDM. Neo gives you the opportunity to have two devices in one, in theory saving some cash, but in doing so, both devices compromise on their overall quality.

With that said, there are a few similar devices on the market, but they’re not as polished as the TDM. version of the device. The HyperGear Flip ($34) headphones have earcups that flip outward to act as external speakers, but the design of the Neo is what makes it so functional.

I think there is a place for the TDM. Neo in most people’s audio setup. The highly innovative design means you get two devices in one, and this is incredibly useful if you’re trying to pack light while traveling. The battery life is impressive too, and you can get good sound quality by making some adjustments in the companion app.

However, I personally think the price tag is a little steep for the quality you’re getting, and the speaker volume doesn’t go high enough for my liking. It’s also annoying that the speaker has to be perfectly balanced to get the best sound, although the carry case and strap make this easier.

Do I think the hybrid device is perfect? No. But do I think we’re now going to see more hybrid audio devices follow in its footsteps? Absolutely!

Ashley is a staff writer on the the Reviews team at Tom’s Guide. She has a master’s degree in Magazine Journalism from Cardiff University and a BA in Journalism, Media and Sociology. She has written for titles including Women’s Health UK, writing health and wellness stories, and Virgin Radio UK, specializing in entertainment news and celebrity interviews. She has reported on a variety of topics including music, literature, motorsport, entertainment and health. She has previously reviewed live music events, books, and wellness products but discovering the top audio equipment on the market is what she does best. When she is not testing out the latest tech, you can find her either curled up with a cup of tea and a good novel or out hiking.

#3268. How Wikipedia’s Editors Keep the Online Encyclopedia Human-Written

The November issue of IEEE Spectrum is here!

AI-generated text is harder to spot, but that hasn’t deterred them

Eliza Strickland is IEEE Spectrum's features editor. She also covers AI and biomedical engineering.

Ellia Lebleu is a cofounder of the WikiProject AI Cleanup effort to keep Wikipedia human-written.

Ellia Lebleu is a founding member of the WikiProject AI Cleanup, a volunteer effort launched in 2023 to find and remove AI-generated material from Wikipedia that breaks the website’s guidelines. When the cleanup began, AI writing was often betrayed by conspicuous clichés. Today, the project’s volunteers are developing tools to detect subtler forms of machine-generated content and debating AI’s role in the world’s most widely used encyclopedia.

When did you realize Wikipedia had a problem with AI-generated material?

Ellia Lebleu: It was around December 2023. A few other editors and I were chatting on Wikipedia’s Discord server, and we had all seen very strange articles with the same odd characteristics. They repeated phrases like “stands as a testament” or “rich cultural heritage.” They sometimes had conclusion sections, or sections called “Why is this important?” That was very typical of ChatGPT in 2023 and early 2024 but very odd for Wikipedia articles—and very easy to spot. Then I decided, let’s create an official project on Wikipedia so more people can deal with this.

Ellia Lebleu Ellia Lebleu is a founding member of the WikiProject AI Cleanup. Lebleu is pursuing a Ph.D. in AI at the Inria Center of the University of Rennes, part of France’s national research institute for digital science and technology.

Ellia Lebleu is a founding member of the WikiProject AI Cleanup. Lebleu is pursuing a Ph.D. in AI at the Inria Center of the University of Rennes, part of France’s national research institute for digital science and technology.

How do editors spot AI-generated writing today?

Lebleu: By 2025, the signs of AI writing were becoming subtler and more structural. For example, AI loves the “rule of three,” negative parallelisms, and other structures of speech that aren’t conclusive by themselves but become meaningful as they accumulate. We also look beyond the article. If someone writes five articles of thousands of words each in 5 minutes, there is reason to suspect AI.

Does the AI problem just appear in the main text, or also in citations?

Lebleu: Fake or misleading citations have become a major worry. Sometimes an AI hallucinates a citation entirely, although that’s much rarer today because of retrieval-augmented generation that allows the AI to find sources. More often, it finds a real source but gets its content completely wrong. AI citations that don’t actually support what is being written are extremely commonplace.

English Wikipedia recently prohibited editors from using LLMs to generate articles. How much AI-generated content is still getting through?

Lebleu: I’ve been working with [AI-detection company] Pangram to estimate the proportion of AI-generated content. I tested it on Wikipedia content from before ChatGPT and found no false positives, so its results provide a very conservative lower bound. In late 2025, it flagged perhaps 20 percent of new articles and drafts as AI-generated. In early 2026, that went down to 15 or 16 percent. But we don’t yet know whether that’s because our recent policies have had an effect or because models are getting more powerful and Pangram hasn’t had time to adapt.

Lebleu: Another Wikipedia editor has made an AI source verifier, which goes through the sources on a page and checks whether they match the claims. Since it is itself an AI model, there is no guarantee that it will be correct every time. But if you want something that works at scale and filters out obvious cases, it’s a good first step. The Wikimedia Foundation is also working on a tool called Paste Check, which can flag text pasted directly from some AI chatbots.

And we’ve seen Claude sometimes say, “I can’t write a Wikipedia article; it would go against Wikipedia’s policies.” If all major AI companies implemented that kind of prompt refusal, it wouldn’t solve the problem entirely, because there are still open-weight models that can be tweaked to avoid restrictions. But it would help with people who use commercial models and aren’t especially familiar with the technology.

Can you tell if the rule prohibiting AI writing is working?

Lebleu: It’s still a little early to tell. We see possible effects, such as prompt refusal and the apparent slight drop in AI-generated content. But again, we don’t yet know if that is because models are getting better or because beginners are learning the rules. The vast majority of AI-generated content is submitted by beginner editors, so we’ve made many efforts to make the rule very visible in welcome messages, editing help, and advice.

What if AI becomes capable of writing truly reliable Wikipedia articles?

Lebleu: That’s one of the big questions we’re facing. When the guideline was passed, it was for very practical reasons: We were flooded with AI content, we didn’t have good tools, and we needed to put a stop to it. But since then, it has taken on a more philosophical dimension. Many people have called Wikipedia “the last good place on the internet.” Being a place that was, in theory, free from AI slop has become part of Wikipedia’s identity.

A lot of Wikipedia’s communication is now centered on the idea that we’re a human-written encyclopedia. Even AI companies find that interesting. It can be valuable to have a purely human-written corpus on which to [train] AI systems. The fact that Wikipedia is still that, and will remain that for at least the near future, makes it a precious resource that isn’t replicated anywhere else.

But will the people who read and contribute to Wikipedia want it to become partially AI-generated if that makes it more comprehensive? We could preserve Wikipedia’s identity as a human-written corpus while also offering an AI-assisted option.

Has Wikipedia reckoned with the idea of “Google Zero”—a possible future in which websites no longer get traffic from Google search?

Lebleu: If everything goes through AI search and websites plummet to zero visibility, how do we expose Wikipedia and show that it can be edited and that people can still contribute? Wikipedia is frequently cited in [Google’s] AI Overviews, but users may only see an AI answer citing Wikipedia. They may not realize that Wikipedia is a living project they can edit and contribute to.

The Wikimedia Foundation is working on an attribution framework that could give AI users more information about the article [being cited]: when it was last edited, how comprehensive it is, whether editors have flagged problems, and perhaps even a call to action. In the future, readers might even contribute through AI models: “The AI cited Wikipedia, but there seems to be an error. Can I make an edit request and add this other source I found?”

I can see a very strong symbiotic relationship between Wikipedia and AI models in the future. I don’t see Wikipedia disappearing, but I can see it taking a very different shape. Yesterday, AI was something to clean up. Today, it’s a tool to help us with the cleanup. Tomorrow, it will be the air we breathe.

A condensed version of this article appears in the November 2026 print issue as “Ellia Lebleu.”

Eliza Strickland is IEEE Spectrum's features editor, where she helps develop and shape the magazine’s longform stories. She also oversees Spectrum's coverage of artificial intelligence and biomedical engineering. She holds a master’s degree in journalism from Columbia University.

I feel like all of us human writers are going to have to grapple with AI-mediated readers, whether we use the AI to augment our content or our readers use AI to engage with our writing. Here's to figuring out together how to ensure our words still shine through the AI layer.

AI slop is a small problem for Wikipedia. The bigger problem is very biased editing on anything with even minimal political implication. And that's a human problem, not AI.

#3267. iPadOS 27.2 adds convenient new multitasking option on iPad

iPadOS 27.2 launched last week with a variety of new features for iPad, including a convenient change for multitasking.

When iPhone Duo first got into users’ hands, several reviews mentioned how the new Split View system felt more intuitive than iPadOS multitasking ever has.

And in iPadOS 27.2, there’s a convenient new multitasking change that’s likely inspired by iPhone Duo.

Apple hasn’t brought over the entire iOS system to the iPad. But it has made one common multitasking feature easier to set up: Split View.

From the official iPadOS 27.2 release notes:

Side-by-side multitasking is easier to set up with the option to choose a second app whenever you tile apps to the left or right with the window controls or menu bar

Starting with iPadOS 26 last year, setting up two apps side-by-side could fairly cumbersome.

You needed to open the first app, resize it, then swipe up from the bottom of the screen to see your other apps, select one, and in many cases manually resize the second app too.

But in iPadOS 27.2, any time you use Apple’s window resizing controls to tile an app left or right, you’ll immediately see the Home Screen and be able to tile a second app with a single tap.

FTA: "Once you master the built-in keyboard shortcuts for app tiling, it becomes even quicker and easier to set up your apps side-by-side."

Ok, great, but…then no one lists these keyboard shortcuts. Sure would have been helpful to paste them in here when talking about new features.

It’s not identical to the iPhone Duo experience, but it’s a lot closer to it than the old system was.

Once you master the built-in keyboard shortcuts for app tiling, it becomes even quicker and easier to set up your apps side-by-side.

#3266. Manfred “Fred” J. Schindler Is 2027 IEEE President-Elect

The November issue of IEEE Spectrum is here!

He has been an active volunteer for more than 30 years

Joanna Goodrich is the associate editor of The Institute.

Manfred “Fred” J. Schindler is the 2027 IEEE president-elect.

IEEE Life Fellow Manfred “Fred” J. Schindler has been elected as the 2027 IEEE president-elect. He will begin serving as president on 1 January 2028.

Schindler, who was nominated by the IEEE Board of Directors, received 16,421 votes in the election. Senior Member David Alan Koehler received 13,874 votes.

Schindler’s Top 3 Goals as President-Elect Strengthen IEEE’s connection with industry by coordinating events across geography, industry, and technology to revitalize professional activities, especially ones for young professionals.Champion the improvement of IEEE’s digital infrastructure to eliminate manual processes and modernize interfaces.Prioritize the advancement of technology to benefit future generations by expanding and supporting IEEE initiatives and programs.

At press time, the results were unofficial until the IEEE Board of Directors accepts the IEEE Teller’s Committee report in November.

Schindler, an expert in microwave semiconductor technology, is an independent consultant supporting clients with technical expertise, due diligence, and project management.

Throughout his career, he led the development of microwave integrated-circuit technology, from lab demonstrations to high-volume commercial products. He has numerous technical publications and holds 11 patents.

Schindler served as CTO of Anlotek, and director of Qorvo and RFMD’s Boston design center. He was applications manager at IBM, engineering manager at ATN Microwave, and a lab manager at Raytheon.

An IEEE volunteer for more than 30 years, Schindler served as the 2024 vice president of IEEE Technical Activities and the 2021–2022 Division IV director. He was chair of the IEEE Conferences Committee from 2015 to 2018 and president of the IEEE Microwave Theory and Technology Society (MTTS) in 2003. He received the society’s 2018 Distinguished Service Award and its 2015 N. Walter Cox Award. His award-winning micro-business column has appeared in IEEE Microwave Magazine since 2011.

He also led the 2025 One IEEE to Enable Strategic Investments in Innovations and Public Imperative Activities adhoc committee.

Schindler is an IEEE–Eta Kappa Nu member and a MTTS honorary life member.

Joanna Goodrich is the associate editor of The Institute, covering the work and accomplishments of IEEE members and IEEE and technology-related events. She has a master's degree in health communications from Rutgers University, in New Brunswick, N.J.

#3265. New report on ‘HomeView Ultra’ product covers features, pricing, more

Apple’s new HomeView product arrives in users’ homes next week, but today a report from The Information outlines what to expect from a larger, high-end ‘HomeView Ultra’ product coming next year.

Today Aaron Tilley at The Information published a report on a forthcoming HomeView product that could be dubbed ‘HomeView Ultra.’

Similar to Mark Gurman’s extensive reporting, Tilley classifies the new home product as a robotics project. He says, “Apple’s new CEO John Ternus wants the company to get serious about robots.”

Per the report, the HomeView Ultra product has “a nine-inch screen that swivels around on an arm and resembles the Pixar lamp.” Tilley writes:

Apple initially began working on the robot in 2019—code-naming it J595—and had modest ambitions for it, envisioning it mostly as a device for video calls. Its robotic arm was intended to allow it to follow someone wherever they were in a room. But hopes for the robot ballooned once Apple executives began wanting to add AI capabilities to it.

The current design for the robot envisions it using a camera and sensors to be fully aware of its environment and act autonomously, allowing it to turn on the lights when someone walks into a room—or perhaps even try to tell a cat to get oﬀ a table. It is meant to be smart enough to avoid accidentally hitting objects around it.

Just get MagSafe going for iPads and create a base for it to attach to plus a HomeView like interface that turns on when attached.

Obviously though Apple wants an exclusive device because adding MagSafe to iPads would allow anyone to make such a base.

And if someone else comes up with an iPad solution it’ll likely get blocked from the App Store.

The report notes that much of the hardware for the product “has been finished for around two years.” Software, however, is keeping the device from shipping. This is due to a more ambitious slate of AI-powered features than was originally envisioned.

Pricing is expected to be “around $1,000” per the report, but it may cost more depending on market prices for components. Tilley spoke to several former employees who said they expect Apple to use ‘HomeView Ultra’ branding for the product. As we’ve seen this fall though, Apple has been hesitant to expand its slate of Ultra products.

As for release timing, Tilley says that “Apple hopes to launch the robot next year. It could push the launch out to 2028 though.”

#3263. Living with Mom and trading on margin. The regular investor gets in on Wall Street's record stock borrowing binge

HOUSTON — During a late night at home in May 2021, Hy Luu, a 29-year-old engineering consultant, was researching how to obtain more capital to invest in shares of Tesla.

That's when he discovered margin investing: the act of borrowing money from a broker to buy securities such as stocks, while using existing investments as collateral. Borrowing would give him more buying power, and he could pay it back as the stock appreciated. The main risk would be a margin call, or having to deposit more money into the account, if its value fell.

It was all too good to be true, Luu thought.

Luu — who lives with his mother, Kim Nguyen, in a three-bedroom, two-bathroom house in Houston — decided to get her opinion on the topic, given that she used to work as an accountant and just so happened to still be awake that evening. The 66-year-old retiree found it interesting.

That was the reassurance he needed, and it wasn't long before he started using margin to invest in Tesla for the first time. A year or so later, he had amassed more than $100,000 of margin debt.

"I went really crazy," he told CNBC in an interview. "The stock was going up, and so I was like, 'There's no way I could lose.'"

After five years of margin investing — including a period in 2022 where he worried that further declines in Tesla could trigger a margin call — Luu is working to pay down his largest margin balance ever. In June, he exercised $165,000 on five Tesla call options and bought 500 shares at $330 per share. After accounting for the cash in his account, this drove his borrowing to more than $156,000.

Tesla swung from below $370 a share to more than $430 during that month.

Between his Tesla investments, his company stock and 401(k) — while subtracting his margin debt as well as other debt he's accumulated, such as his car loan and student loans — Luu's net worth has skyrocketed to more than $800,000 from negative territory seven years ago.

"I'm very close to becoming a millionaire," the investor said. He did stress, "What I'm doing is risky. I don't recommend anyone do it."

Yet, Luu has found himself part of a growing trend taking hold in the market.

Retail investors like Luu are borrowing more and more money to invest. Robinhood's margin book grew to a record $21.6 billion in the second quarter, up 127% year over year and a 332% increase from the $5 billion seen in Q2 2024. To margin invest on the platform, eligible users must have a portfolio value of at least $2,000.

"Robinhood has made a really concerted effort to go after customers that are actively using margin because they're the most active traders," said Devin Ryan, head of financial technology research at Citizens.

Brokerage firms can benefit from margin investing by collecting interest on margin loans, while highly active customers can also generate additional trading-related revenue.

"If you look at the offers that Robinhood has had in the market over the past couple of years, it's been targeting those customers with obviously transfer bonuses, but also very low margin rates, very high yields on their cash," Ryan said.

To be sure, other parts of Robinhood's business are also growing, including retirement assets — which have nearly quadrupled in the last two years.

Another factor fueling the rise in margin investing is easier access through smartphones, according to Ryan.

"Having very little friction in investing and having everything at your fingertips, and then having a really seamless mobile experience where it's not clunky, I think, plays a big part of that," he said.

A Robinhood spokesperson told CNBC its products are designed to appeal to a number of customers, saying that "we don't believe it's accurate to characterize" its transfer promotions as specifically targeting "active traders who are trading on margin or may trade on margin." The company said it tries to "meet users where they are," and they "reject any implication" that the company is "encouraging risky trading."

Robinhood's margin debt isn't the only one reaching records. Total margin debt hit an all-time high of around $1.5 trillion in June, per the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority, which incorporates data on both institutional investors such as hedge funds and retail investors.

Not all of that debt is driven by fresh borrowing due to new borrowing decisions. For example, as equities rise in value, an investor may need to cover a short position that's been marked to market, or valued at its current price.

Nonetheless, Sam Huszczo, chief investment officer at SGH Wealth Management, thinks the market's bull run — which has seen multiple record highs this year alone — is feeding a shift in investor psychology, and margin debt is one sign.

"That's greed," the founder said, adding that it's "not everywhere" in the market, but it's "certainly creeping into pockets."

"Margin, that's only the tip of the iceberg of what we can see," he continued. "Fear of missing out is just the emotion of jealousy with a brokerage account."

Huszczo considers the market to actually be "way healthier" than people think. Though he recognizes that increasing margin debt and the rise of risky assets such as leveraged ETFs inject more fragility in the system.

"People need to differentiate between what's a legitimate momentum growth investment and what's reckless chasing," Huszczo also said.

Huszczo shares the commonly held belief among financial advisors that investors' portfolios shouldn't be overly concentrated in one stock or even one sector.

Yet Luu has been zeroed in on Tesla ever since he bought his first share in late 2019. Earlier that year, he had started his current job — a time when he knew nothing about investing, he said. It wasn't until a co-worker told him to download Robinhood months later that he began looking into stocks and other assets.

"I started making money, and I quickly learned, 'Now I'm making money, what do I do with it?'" he said. "I started investing in index funds and even in crypto, and then I did the math. I looked at the returns, and I was like, 'This is very slow returns. I'm never gonna reach retirement, financial independence until like 65.'"

Little did he know that a decision he had made that summer would become his guiding light.

"I was choosing between a Honda Civic and a Tesla Model 3, and my friend, he scheduled a test drive for me to drive the Model 3," Luu said. "My plan was only to go into it just to test drive it. I wasn't going to buy anything. I wasn't going to put in any reservation. Long story short, after the test drive, I put in my reservation the same day, and I got the car like two weeks later."

Seeing the value the car provides in his life, Luu said he can envision a future where electric and autonomous vehicles are commonplace. Because of how much he believes in that future, he considers Tesla the "easiest" investment he's made, and over the course of seven years of investing in the company, he has generally held his shares.

However, things got a bit more difficult with his strategy when Tesla shares began falling in 2022, putting him in the vulnerable position of potentially receiving a margin call. 2022 was Tesla's worst year on record, with the stock finishing off the year at $123.18 after a roughly 65% decline.

In search of more capital, Luu made a serious financial decision with his mother's approval.

"I refinanced the house to get access to an extra $30,000 of capital, and I used that to pay down my margin debt," he said.

Luu understands the level of risk that accompanies trading with margin. Because he's been using margin for most of the nearly seven years he's been investing in Tesla, he has deemed his investing strategy "gambling with an asterisk."

For now, it has paid off. In the last five years, Tesla shares have risen more than 43% to $375. However, the volatile stock is about 25% off of its all-time high near $499.

"It's very easy to see it as gambling, because obviously all your money is in one stock, and that's inherently risky," he said. "But the reason why I say there's nuance to it is because it's a matter of investing temperament, financial discipline and time horizon."

With a time horizon of "many decades," a temperament he labels as "very calm and collected" and a "very high" conviction in Tesla, Luu believes he's "at no risk of panic selling," even when the market tanks.

Still, the situation points out another danger: Missing an opportunity to make an investment when an equity is undervalued. When Luu was scrambling to raise funds to meet his margin obligation, it reduced his flexibility to purchase more Tesla shares at the lower price.

Margin levels this high have been followed by risk-off periods in equities.

Whenever monthly margin debt has grown above 45% year over year since 1960, there were declines in the stock market five out of six times, data from Fundstrat Global Advisors shows. June's margin debt record came in at 49%, but the S&P 500 has still added more than 13% in 2026. A swing into the red by year-end in accordance with this historic pattern would be a dramatic move — one that would be considered highly unusual for the stock market.

The firm also found that the median performance for S&P 500 forward returns following a breakout of 40% year-over-year margin debt growth has been worse off 12 months later as opposed to one month after it. To be exact, the S&P 500's median 12-month forward return is a 4.2% decline, while the median one-month return is a drop of 2.2%.

In essence, the more rapidly margin debt rises, the worse it is for S&P 500 returns over 12 months.

While margin debt doesn't necessarily cause S&P 500 declines, it can exacerbate existing moves to the downside if there's a significant amount of leverage in the market, said Hardika Singh, economic strategist at Fundstrat.

"The premise of gains beget gains, it turns into losses beget losses, and that's what's troublesome," Singh said. "You have these losses, they keep piling up, and then the stock gets sold, and everyone's starting to close out their position, and it becomes this huge train wreck that's very hard to stop, and it adds a lot of volatility to the market."

Then again, Singh sees why investors like Luu are leaning into such a risky strategy. "No one ever got rich by diversifying," she said.

Luu, who said he's been a "hobbyist" from an early age, has folded in investing as one of his many hobbies, which include activities like climbing and playing guitar. It's become such a hobby that he's created his own social media account detailing his investing journey.

Even if Luu reaches his financial goals, he "wouldn't ever stop investing," he said. Instead, he said he "would probably start investing in SpaceX."

It's not just Luu who views trading as a hobby.

Fundstrat's Singh explained that American traders, particularly younger ones, feel they have to take bigger risks to get ahead. She said it's part of a broader trend dubbed financial nihilism, in which young investors grappling with a tough job market and high inflation turn to less-stable investing tools.

"It makes a lot of sense why individuals, specifically retail investors, keep gravitating towards this margin debt," the economic strategist added. "This is like a drug, and I think people just can't get enough of it in this economy."

Kevin Davis, a 59-year-old retail investor who made a living as a rapper in the 1980s and '90s before becoming a stock broker, believes the risks with leveraged trading outweigh the rewards.

"It's gambling. You're borrowing money you don't have, and so if it goes the other way, now you have a clock on your money, and it's ticking," said Davis, who owns an investing technology platform. "The market's not going to save you. It never does."

"Don't play the margin game," the Florida resident warned.

Luu became an engineering consultant because his father, who died of lung cancer in 2012, exposed him to computing. His mother said that between her two sons, Luu most resembles his father not only in terms of his features but also his character.

Reflecting on what her late husband might have thought about Luu's investing pursuits, Nguyen paused for a moment, holding a slight smile.

She then said, "He would've said he's proud of him."

— CNBC's Charlotte Morabito and Deena Zaidi contributed to this report.

#3261. Why Engineers Should Brave Capitol Hill

The November issue of IEEE Spectrum is here!

Congress needs accurate technical insights

Lucas Laursen is the technology policy editor at IEEE Spectrum.

During this year’s Congressional Visits Day, Nikhil Jathar [second from left] and three other IEEE members met with Nile Whitmore [middle], a legislative assistant for Representative Greg Casar (D-Texas).

When San Antonio–based software engineer Nikhil Jathar first went to Washington, D.C., to advocate for federal support for technology education and research funding, he was in awe of the opportunity. It was spring of 2025, not long after Jathar settled in the United States from India, when he got an invitation to join the annual Congressional Visits Day organized by IEEE-USA.

“My first reaction was, ‘Wow, I get to visit Congress,’ ” says Jathar, CTO of AvanSaber, a business software company he cofounded in 2014. At the time, he did not have a specific lobbying position on behalf of the company. But he was intrigued by the invitation—which goes out to all U.S. IEEE members—and as he read more about congressional visits, his motivation deepened. He realized: “I need to try this. I want to see where it goes.”

What’s Your Ask? Congressional staffers expect clarity from advocates. Be clear on what you plan to ask for when you arrive. Here are some common options:Cosponsor (or oppose) an existing bill or amendment.Preserve, remove, or modify legislative text in a bill under consideration.Add language to an appropriations bill or committee report.Ask a federal agency a specific oversight question.Request a briefing, hearing, Government Accountability Office review, or stakeholder roundtable.Encourage an agency to clarify a technical rule.

Congressional staffers expect clarity from advocates. Be clear on what you plan to ask for when you arrive. Here are some common options:

Congressional staffers say they welcome the knowledge and perspective that engineers like Jathar and other visitors from beyond Washington, D.C., provide. It’s also important for those visitors to be clear on what they are advocating for. One staffer for the House Committee on Science, Space, and Technology, who agreed to speak anonymously due to the office’s media policy, says, “Ideas for new policies come from multiple places. It could begin at the [legislator] or staff level, an ask from a constituent, or needs from industry. It’s up to us to figure out what would do the most good,” the staffer said. “For instance, if you leave it to the lobbyists, they’re understandably going to do what’s in their clients’ interests.”

For engineers in the United States, speaking with elected representatives is an effective way to shape key policies, but it takes some preparation and the right approach, as Jathar learned over the course of two visits.

Congress’s job is to act on behalf of the people, and it has rules for how people can lobby it. It distinguishes between broader advocacy—conversations between constituents and U.S. representatives—and professional lobbying, which involves paid professionals and is governed by the Lobbying Disclosure Act. Many professional groups like IEEE also organize congressional visits for their members. Those visits can be subject to lobbying rules, so the organizers told Jathar that: “You are representing the organization, not your own views.” He would need to stick to the talking points IEEE-USA had prepared for all its participants, regardless of their specialty, to promote across several congressional offices.

On Jathar’s first visit, those organizational talking points included advocating for funding smart grids, authorizing Department of Energy research, and investing in STEM education. That represents one of the trade-offs of access in Washington. IEEE-USA’s priorities didn’t all overlap directly with Jathar’s work, but they were broad enablers of science and technology and, he says, “STEM education funding is close to my heart.”

Anyone can approach their representatives in Washington with their personal priorities, Jathar notes, but given how pressed for time congressional staff are, they are more likely to prioritize a meeting that represents the views of as many of their constituents as possible. “I could have gone outside the IEEE structure,” Jathar says, but congressional staff “are more likely to listen if you are part of a much bigger organization.”

For Jathar’s first congressional visit, organizers assigned him to call on the offices of several representatives from both political parties based on where he lives: Representatives Greg Casar (D-Texas), Lloyd Doggett (D-Texas), and Barry Moore (R-Ala.). “Meeting a staffer or a senior member from their office is good. They tend to relate to these issues more than a representative, because a representative has 10 different high-level things they have to worry about whereas the staffer can be more focused on the policy details,” Jathar says.

A typical visit like this may last anywhere from 15 minutes to an hour, so Jathar kept his talking points simple and short. “First and foremost you’re gonna get a very small window,” he says, “Make sure you’ve got everything ready to present in bullet points and not a lot of jargon. You can always bring that out later if they ask more questions.” Simple visual aids, in the form of one-page handouts, may be helpful for communicating numeric or technical information, too.

“If you leave it to the lobbyists, they’re understandably going to do what’s in their clients’ interests.”–Staffer for the House Committee on Science, Space, and Technology

The House Science Committee staffer agrees: “I prefer meetings where people know what they want and know what we’re doing in Congress.” In addition to having a clear request, the staffer says engineers and other advocates should keep track of where Congress is in its cycle: Is it appropriations season, and when is the next budget being set? How far along is a given piece of legislation in the process, and what is realistic to change at that point?

During Jathar’s 2025 visit to one Capitol Hill office, he learned firsthand the importance of preparation. For one of the three representatives he visited, staff politely pointed out that the legislator they worked for was not on the committee with jurisdiction over the IEEE-USA talking point they were discussing. “They explained that there are only certain things [the legislator] can do on that issue and that there are other people we need to talk to, to achieve more,” Jathar recalls.

Earlier this year, Jathar decided to go back to Capitol Hill with his newfound knowledge, again within the framework of an IEEE-USA visit. This time he was able to provide something else legislative staff want from engineers: authoritative technical knowledge.

“When I introduced myself as a software developer to one staffer, his first question was, ‘Do you think AI will replace coders?’ ” Jathar says. The conversation went back and forth, with the staffer asking Jathar and his other engineering companions questions. Jathar went on to explain that his company developed an open-source business-management software it calls ERPClaw, designed to be used with AI agents such as OpenClaw. That led naturally to discussing the role of open source in AI, which plays a role in one of IEEE-USA’s proposals for democratizing AI. This time Jathar was able to align his organization’s advocacy with his expertise and the staffer’s areas of interest.

It’s too soon to know what legislative impact that advocacy might have, but it’s the sort of informed, relevant proposal that legislative staff seek out. “The people who build trust have more cachet with congressional staff because they’ve asked for something that’s reasonably thought out,” the House Science Committee staffer says. In turn, congressional staffers can advocate better within their offices for policies brought to them by people they trust.

And talking about the issues you care the most about can deepen that trust. The House Science Committee staffer once visited Congress as an advocate before switching to the other side of the table. On that visit, as on Jathar’s, the professional society organizing the visit provided a pitch. “I was making a pitch that was given to me without a lot of personal buy-in,” the staffer says. Instead, “you should feel emotionally connected to any issue you’re advocating for.”

Jathar’s support for the open-source movement is like that. Open source gives smaller companies a foundation they can adapt and build upon, while allowing other developers to extend that work. “We can progress a lot faster,” Jathar says. “I’m not doing it only because it’s good for my business, but because I feel it’s good for any technological advancement.”

Lucas Laursen is the technology policy editor at IEEE Spectrum. He covers how emerging technologies are changing the balance of power between companies, governments, and individuals. The rest of the time, he worries about his own balance on a bicycle, skis, or the side of a mountain.

I found it difficult to get answers from legislative offices, so I'd love to hear what's missing in this story from any legislative staffers either here in the comments or at my email address (on our About page). I also know that things work somewhat differently in each country--are there readers in India or Germany or Chile who might be able to share their experiences working with lawmakers there?

#3259. Could Investing in Moderna's Stock Double Your Money?

The healthcare stock has generated massive returns this year and may still have room to rise even higher in the future.

Moderna (MRNA -0.40%) has generated terrific gains for investors this year, as the stock has skyrocketed more than 650% entering trading this week. It's been on a tremendous run due to the excitement around its cancer vaccine, intismeran.

The vaccine isn't approved yet, however. And that also means the business may be on the cusp of generating significant revenue in the future, due to the promising treatment. Although the stock's up big this year, could investing in Moderna now still enable investors to double their money? Here's why that may not be an unrealistic scenario.

Recent clinical trial numbers involving intismeran and Merck's top cancer drug, Keytruda, have lit a fire under Moderna's stock this year. The combination has been highly effective in reducing the risk of death or recurrence in melanoma patients.

But the hope is that intismeran may work in other settings as well. Merck and Moderna are evaluating it for other cancers, including non-small cell lung cancer -- multiple late-stage trials are ongoing in this area.

If there are promising results from other studies, that could heighten hopes that intismeran may be useful for not just one but many types of cancers, likely making it a game changer for Moderna's business, which has been struggling to grow in recent years.

What may surprise investors is that although Moderna's been red-hot this year, it's still not as high as it was in 2021, when the business was booming due to robust demand for its COVID vaccine. Over the past five years, Moderna's stock is still in negative territory, down around 36% as of the end of last week.

It's been a rough ride for investors who have hung on since then. The good news is that the business looks to have a brighter path ahead. While intismeran hasn't obtained approval just yet, it appears highly likely that will happen given its strong clinical trial results. And if intismeran obtains approval for treating multiple cancers, then it may indeed be just what's needed for the healthcare stock to skyrocket even further in value.

For Moderna's stock to double, its valuation would climb to around $180 billion. At that level, the business would likely need to generate strong numbers beyond just having high expectations. Thus, it may take a while for it to get there. Moderna has plenty of potential, but this may not be an appropriate option for investors with a low risk tolerance.

David Jagielski, CPA has no position in any of the stocks mentioned. The Motley Fool has positions in and recommends Merck and Moderna. The Motley Fool has a disclosure policy.

#3258. Junk bonds are 'flashing yellow.' Watch these warning signs

Cracks are forming in the junk bond market as investors demand higher payouts for owning the market's riskiest debt. It isn't time to ditch high-yield bonds, but investors should pay attention to the warning signs.

High-yield bonds now yield 8.1%, up from 7.22% a month ago. The increase reflects a jump in yields across the curve as investors bake in more inflation from high energy prices and other pressures, including concern about the deficit — hitting nearly $2 trillion in the fiscal year that ended Sept. 30.

The high-yield market is also showing stress on the credit side with spreads recently widening to levels not seen since April, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis. Credit spreads are the difference in yield between the bonds and Treasurys of similar maturities. Wider spreads mean investors are demanding higher yields for holding corporate debt, viewing it as riskier.

Spreads are at 315 basis points in the overall high-yield market, higher than a year ago but still below levels in March when they reached 346 bps. One basis point equals one one-hundredth of a percent, or 0.01%.

The high-yield market consists of bonds rated BB+ by S&P and Fitch and Ba1 and under by Moody's. The lowest-rated cohort, CCC and below, has seen the most movement with spreads climbing dramatically over the past year to roughly 1,250 bps.

Right now, the high-yield market is "flashing yellow" but is "far from red," said Michael Arone, chief investment strategist at State Street Investment Management.

It makes sense that investors are demanding more compensation for taking on additional credit risk as borrowing costs rise, he said.

Yields are elevated across the board with the 10-year Treasury reaching its highest level since 2002 earlier in the week.

"The bigger question is whether this is simply a repricing of interest rate risk, or the beginning of a more fundamental reassessment of credit quality," Arone said.

He's in a wait-and-see mode since earnings are still growing, interest-coverage ratios remain good, and while default rates have ticked up some, he believes it is not concerning.

That said, the starting point in spreads is likely weighing on investors' psyche, since they are still low by historical standards.

"There's a small margin of error here, which I also think raises the anxiety level," Arone explained. "The compensation that investors are receiving for taking on this credit risk isn't overwhelming relative to history, and therefore subtle changes in credit spreads can be concerning."

While there may be concerns about part of the lower-rated market, the overall high-yield market is in good fundamental shape.

In fact, credit quality is at a record high, with BB bonds making up over 60% of the market compared with 38% prior to the global financial crisis, said Kelley Gerrity, a fixed income strategist at Morgan Stanley Investment Management.

"We've had higher-quality companies coming in, and with higher rates now, you also have more discipline from companies that are more indebted ... just because of the higher cost of capital, so that actually is creating a bit of a healthier picture as well," she said.

The lowest tier of high yield has always been more speculative, since the bonds have a higher default risk. Therefore, it's no surprise that they are the ones seeing the most widening in spreads, said Collin Martin, head of fixed income research and strategy at the Schwab Center for Financial Research.

The overall move in high-yield spreads have been "orderly," he said. "Are there cracks forming? I think the cracks are logical cracks with the lowest-rated bonds and it's too early to say that it's spreading to the broad credit market."

In addition, fluctuations within the CCC-rated and lower spreads have been idiosyncratic, Gerrity added. Morgan Stanley recently broke down the spreads in the lowest cohort into two buckets: performing assets and non-performing assets, which are defined as spreads above 1,000 bps.

The non-performing spread to worst is 2,818 bps, while the performing bucket — the biggest piece of the CCC market — is 461 bps, she said.

"It is isolated," she said. "I'm not necessarily sure that that will go away anytime soon, but it doesn't tell the story of overall concern and flashing caution for credit markets right now."

For now, investors should remain selective within higher yield, Gerrity advised.

"We're looking for the best relative value opportunities, and we think that exists within that single-B cohort, and so we're leaning into that," she said.

Investors should be concerned if there is a steep widening in the broader high-yield market.

But there's scant evidence of stress in the BB cohort. Spreads in that group are at 194 bps, up from 179 bps a year ago — although the move hasn't been in a straight line.

"We're going to be focusing our attention on what are considered some stronger businesses," Martin said. "If we start to see the markets demand higher spreads there also, that's what we'll be looking at to see if risks are really rising."

It's also important to understand that the Federal Reserve is raising rates in a strong economic environment, said R.J. Gallo, chief investment officer of global fixed income at Federated Hermes. The central bank is concerned about an inflation problem amid high fossil fuel prices due to the Iran war, while growth has been stronger than expected, he noted.

"With growth being good as the reason that the Fed is hiking, then you wouldn't expect high yield to blow out because growth means revenues stay up, means cash flow and profitability stays up," he explained.

High yield becomes a disaster when the economy is heading into a sharp economic downturn, Gallo said.

"That's when spreads really widen out," he said. "But a recession is not the odds-on bet. Now, talk to me in six months if the Fed keeps hiking over and over, if oil prices stay high for longer, well, then maybe we will start to wonder."

#3255. Why AI Can’t Replace Engineering Teams

The November issue of IEEE Spectrum is here!

How to convince your boss LLMs can’t do it all

Brian Jenney is the owner of Parsity, a program that helps engineers through hands-on training.

This article is crossposted from IEEE Spectrum’s careers newsletter. Sign up now to get insider tips, expert advice, and practical strategies, written in partnership with tech career development company Parsity and delivered to your inbox for free!

If you’re an engineer, you may feel like your skills aren’t commanding the premium they once did. Many engineers have faced layoffs or restructuring. But even for those of us who still have jobs, something corrosive is happening. You may have heard some version of this:

“ChatGPT answered that in five seconds. Why can’t you?”

Or, “I made this app in a weekend. Why is our team taking so long?”

I worked on a team where leadership said things like this directly to engineers. This was in 2024 and 2025, when the AI craze was in full swing and Claude and ChatGPT adoption was rising.

Generative AI (and the marketing behind it) gives people the illusion that the work is simpler than it is. A working demo hides complexity, and once someone has a website that works, they may decide they no longer need engineers, or start to distrust the ones they do have.

Some CEOs want to believe they can replace an engineering team with a few sexy prompts. Many companies also want them to believe this.

That website works great in the demo—under specific conditions and without users with thumbs for fingers. Then it has to plug into a system with millions of lines of old code, satisfy legal requirements, meet accessibility standards, and be delivered in a complex deployment process.

Thinking that writing code was the only bottleneck for deploying new software is like the Titanic seeing the tip of the iceberg and assuming there was nothing underneath it.

Engineers have a unique position in the AI space, because you have the capacity to understand how these models work much better than the average person. Use this to your advantage.

Learn how AI models work. If you can’t already explain that LLMs are probabilistic, what tokens are, or why training data matters, spend a weekend fixing that. You don’t need to become a full-blown AI researcher. A few fundamentals will put you ahead of most people making the AI decisions.

Teach upward. Turn that knowledge into teaching moments for the people who lead you. Explain the limits of these tools, and why a demo and a production system are different animals. It keeps people from truly believing that a notebook full of prompts can replace an engineering team.

Consider the criticism of today’s processes. Some of what we do has been treated as ceremony for too long. Be willing to say, “you know what, maybe you’re right, this process is too slow for the speed we can work at now.” Conceding that earns you the credibility to defend the steps that matter.

I still believe that speed at the cost of everything else is harmful—but that’s a topic for another time.

Find your voice. Engineers at the forefront of AI adoption need to push back and explain why we do things the way we do. Nobody else in the room is going to do it for us.

Your goal, in my opinion, is to save your organization from buying into the hype so much that they chase the wrong thing. Our job, before and after AI, is building safe and useful products for human beings, and engineers are still best suited for that.

The need to educate engineering students about ethics and social responsibility is widely recognized, but today’s curricula often miss the mark. Three professors propose a new approach: adding ethics training directly to core technical coursework.

Looking for a career in quantum computing hardware? An IBM spin-off called Anderon could receive up to $1 billion in funding from the U.S. CHIPS and Science Act for its quantum foundry, established earlier this year. Could Anderon do for quantum hardware what TSMC did for conventional chips?

When Gurmeet Saran joined Anthropic’s technical staff in 2025, he entered a role focused on a key question: How do you know whether you can trust a chatbot like Claude? Learn more about Saran’s path and his work at the AI company.

Brian Jenney is the owner of Parsity, an online education platform that helps people break into AI and modern software roles through project-based learning and one-on-one mentorship with senior developers. Parsity helps career changers transition into software by focusing on practical skills, real-world systems, and the kind of experience companies actually look for.Outside Parsity, Brian works a senior software engineer in the SF Bay Area.Brian is also a father of three, and when he’s not working with students or building programs, you might catch him running around Lake Merritt in Oakland, California.

#3254. Here's Exactly How Much $5,000 in Procter & Gamble Has Paid Out in Dividends Since 2020

Procter & Gamble has one of the most impressive dividend histories.

It's hard to believe that the pandemic started more than six years ago. There was human suffering, of course, and businesses closed due to stay-at-home orders.

However, looking back on those bleak times, it does show the power of buying high-quality, dividend-paying companies and holding on to them. If you'd invested $5,000 into market leader Procter & Gamble (PG +1.23%), here's how much you'd have collected in dividends.

Beyond that, here's why you should continue owning the company's shares.

The stock price closed Dec. 31, 2019, at $124.90. If you'd decided to buy $5,000 worth of Procter & Gamble's shares before heading out to a New Year's Eve party, you'd have purchased 40 shares.

You'd have received higher dividend payouts each year. In fact, Procter & Gamble has one of the most impressive dividend histories. As of this year, the company has paid dividends for 136 years and raised them annually for the last 70 straight years. That makes Procter & Gamble a Dividend King, an impressive group of companies that has increased dividends for at least 50 straight years.

During 2020, you'd have received $124.72 in total payments. And that figure grew. From 2021 through today, the company paid $136, $144.39, $149.42, $158.41, $167.08, and $172.89 for those 40 shares. That totals about $1,053.

The first quarterly dividend you received was $0.7459 per share, and the latest one was $1.0885 per share. That's 46% growth.

Companies can retain earnings or pay them out in dividends. Fortunately, Procter & Gamble has ample earnings to do both.

That's because the company sells essential, everyday products that have leading market shares. This includes shampoo, razors, toothpaste, detergent, and diapers. Consumer staples such as these remain in demand regardless of the state of the economy or people's personal financial situations.

Procter & Gamble continues to grow sales and earnings. The company's fiscal first-quarter sales, adjusted to remove foreign-currency translations and acquisitions/divestitures, grew a steady 4% year over year.

Importantly, 2.4 percentage points came from higher volume, and a changing mix added 1.1 percentage points. Higher prices only added 0.4 percentage points. Core earnings per share increased 1%.

However, management projects this year's earnings per share will increase by up to 3%, with sales growing 1% to 3%. While that might not sound impressive, it comes in the face of cost pressures. Long term, the steady demand should translate into higher earnings and dividends.

That means shareholders can rely on higher dividends for the foreseeable future.
